query:
Context. A university lab runs an AMAZEMET rePOWDER ultrasonic atomizer at about 1400 m altitude (room
pressure about 850-865 mbar). A 0.3-1.1 kg charge (aluminium alloys, and copper alloys such as
nickel-aluminium bronze UNS C63000 poured at about 1300 C) is induction-melted in a graphite crucible,
pushed through a 0.5 mm nozzle by argon over-pressure, and falls onto a plate vibrating at 40 kHz that
breaks it into powder (d50 roughly 100 um on good runs). Powder falls through a water-cooled stainless
cone under the chamber into a collection container that hangs from the cone's outlet flange on a
hinged clamp (ISO-KF style with a centring ring and O-ring, or possibly sanitary tri-clamp; size about
DN40-50, being confirmed). The chamber is evacuated to about 10 mbar absolute and backfilled with argon
several times, then runs at about +150 mbar gauge; a mechanical relief valve opens at +0.8 bar.
The stock container, top to bottom: the flange on a short neck, a conical reducer, a valve body with a
lever-operated flap valve whose seat is an EPDM ring, a borosilicate(?) glass tube about 100 mm across
in a perforated steel guard, sealed by elastomer rings in grooves of a top and a bottom stainless plate,
and four tie rods. A curved stainless splash plate sits in the bore at the top. The manufacturer also
supplies protective "shields" that fit in the cone; on the failed run they were not fitted and the
splash plate was in backwards.

The failure (Nov 13 2026): the plate barely atomized, so most of an 816 g C63000 charge left it as 1-3 mm
shot, still partly liquid when it reached the container about 0.4 s later. Bronze piled up at the
container's entrance; the glass glowed orange; the EPDM valve seat burned (white crust, smoke out of
the joint); the seals under the glass were damaged; the glass cracked at its top rim. Good runs never
damaged the container. The manufacturer says a "much simpler metal cup, without the glass" exists
(a stainless tube with a separate sanitary butterfly valve), and that in their own lab they mostly use
"the simple stainless steel" tube because it is easier to make and clean, but its delivery date is
unknown. The lab wants to build its own container within days to a few weeks, glass or metal.

The lab's design so far (to be reviewed, not assumed correct):
A. All-metal, catalogue parts only: a 316L ISO-KF full nipple (bore about 48 mm, 200-250 mm long) hung
   from the cone with the existing clamp; a KF blank flange at the bottom with a stainless centring ring
   and FKM O-ring; a drop-in 304/316 sacrificial liner sleeve in the top bore so that hot metal cannot
   touch the top O-ring; a loose copper or steel "catch puck" at the bottom to soak up heat and keep the
   pile off the bottom joint; Type K thermocouples clamped on the outside at the top flange and near the
   bottom, read by a panel meter with an alarm; no valve (a KF blank and clamp go on the top after
   removal), or a full-port valve whose seats are hidden behind the ball when open.
B. All-metal, turned and TIG-welded: one 316L vessel (KF weld stub, a 63-76 mm tube, a 10 mm welded
   bottom, no bottom seal), with an internal shoulder that locates the sacrificial liner.
C. Glass rebuild: the stock plates, valve and tie rods with a fused-quartz tube in place of the
   borosilicate, FKM or silicone seals, and a stainless liner sleeve that covers the glass rim and the
   top seal.

Find precedents: published designs, manuals, theses, patents or incident reports for powder
collection canisters, cans or cyclones under metal atomizers (gas, ultrasonic, centrifugal, plasma),
especially how they are protected from unatomized molten metal, shot or splats, what materials and
seals they use, whether they have isolation valves, how they are cooled or instrumented, and any
failures where hot metal reached the collection container, melted seals or cracked glass. Include
lab-scale and university-built atomizers. Give citations with DOIs or URLs.
task_summary: Survey Precedents For Powder Collection Canisters Under Metal Atomizers Including Materials Seals Failures

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available
        - NO_LONGER_AVAILABLE: No longer available
        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care
        - SCREENING: Screening
        - HEALTH_SERVICES_RESEARCH: Health Services Research
        - BASIC_SCIENCE: Basic Science
        - DEVICE_FEASIBILITY: Device Feasibility
        - OTHER: Other

    InterventionType:
        - BEHAVIORAL: Behavioral interventions
        - BIOLOGICAL: Biological interventions
        - COMBINATION_PRODUCT: Combination product interventions
        - DEVICE: Device interventions
        - DIAGNOSTIC_TEST: Diagnostic test interventions
        - DIETARY_SUPPLEMENT: Dietary supplement interventions
        - DRUG: Drug interventions
        - GENETIC: Genetic interventions
        - PROCEDURE: Procedure interventions
        - RADIATION: Radiation interventions
        - OTHER: Other interventions

    DesignAllocation:
        - RANDOMIZED: Randomized allocation
        - NON_RANDOMIZED: Non-randomized allocation
        - NA: Not applicable

    InterventionalAssignment:
        - SINGLE_GROUP: Single group assignment
        - PARALLEL: Parallel assignment
        - CROSSOVER: Crossover assignment
        - FACTORIAL: Factorial assignment
        - SEQUENTIAL: Sequential assignment

    ObservationalModel:
        - COHORT: Cohort
        - CASE_CONTROL: Case-Control
        - CASE_ONLY: Case-Only
        - CASE_CROSSOVER: Case-Crossover
        - ECOLOGIC_OR_COMMUNITY: Ecologic or Community
        - FAMILY_BASED: Family-Based
        - DEFINED_POPULATION: Defined Population
        - NATURAL_HISTORY: Natural History
        - OTHER: Other

    DesignMasking:
        - NONE: None (Open Label)
        - SINGLE: Single
        - DOUBLE: Double
        - TRIPLE: Triple
        - QUADRUPLE: Quadruple

    WhoMasked:
        - PARTICIPANT: Participant
        - CARE_PROVIDER: Care Provider

        - OUTCOMES_ASSESSOR: Outcomes Assessor

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

Search for papers in Google Scholar for you to look at.

Can be called repeatedly with identical parameters to retrieve more results (max 2 repeats).
A short summary of the retrieved papers will be returned, but to examine the full content of each paper,
you must use the gather_evidence tool.

info.name: open_targets_search

Search for disease-target associations from OpenTargets database.

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string encoding an object with an "objectives" list;
never pass objectives separately.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?

Use the tools to answer the question: Context. A university lab runs an AMAZEMET rePOWDER ultrasonic atomizer at about 1400 m altitude (room
pressure about 850-865 mbar). A 0.3-1.1 kg charge (aluminium alloys, and copper alloys such as
nickel-aluminium bronze UNS C63000 poured at about 1300 C) is induction-melted in a graphite crucible,
pushed through a 0.5 mm nozzle by argon over-pressure, and falls onto a plate vibrating at 40 kHz that
breaks it into powder (d50 roughly 100 um on good runs). Powder falls through a water-cooled stainless
cone under the chamber into a collection container that hangs from the cone's outlet flange on a
hinged clamp (ISO-KF style with a centring ring and O-ring, or possibly sanitary tri-clamp; size about
DN40-50, being confirmed). The chamber is evacuated to about 10 mbar absolute and backfilled with argon
several times, then runs at about +150 mbar gauge; a mechanical relief valve opens at +0.8 bar.
The stock container, top to bottom: the flange on a short neck, a conical reducer, a valve body with a
lever-operated flap valve whose seat is an EPDM ring, a borosilicate(?) glass tube about 100 mm across
in a perforated steel guard, sealed by elastomer rings in grooves of a top and a bottom stainless plate,
and four tie rods. A curved stainless splash plate sits in the bore at the top. The manufacturer also
supplies protective "shields" that fit in the cone; on the failed run they were not fitted and the
splash plate was in backwards.

The failure (Nov 13 2026): the plate barely atomized, so most of an 816 g C63000 charge left it as 1-3 mm
shot, still partly liquid when it reached the container about 0.4 s later. Bronze piled up at the
container's entrance; the glass glowed orange; the EPDM valve seat burned (white crust, smoke out of
the joint); the seals under the glass were damaged; the glass cracked at its top rim. Good runs never
damaged the container. The manufacturer says a "much simpler metal cup, without the glass" exists
(a stainless tube with a separate sanitary butterfly valve), and that in their own lab they mostly use
"the simple stainless steel" tube because it is easier to make and clean, but its delivery date is
unknown. The lab wants to build its own container within days to a few weeks, glass or metal.

The lab's design so far (to be reviewed, not assumed correct):
A. All-metal, catalogue parts only: a 316L ISO-KF full nipple (bore about 48 mm, 200-250 mm long) hung
   from the cone with the existing clamp; a KF blank flange at the bottom with a stainless centring ring
   and FKM O-ring; a drop-in 304/316 sacrificial liner sleeve in the top bore so that hot metal cannot
   touch the top O-ring; a loose copper or steel "catch puck" at the bottom to soak up heat and keep the
   pile off the bottom joint; Type K thermocouples clamped on the outside at the top flange and near the
   bottom, read by a panel meter with an alarm; no valve (a KF blank and clamp go on the top after
   removal), or a full-port valve whose seats are hidden behind the ball when open.
B. All-metal, turned and TIG-welded: one 316L vessel (KF weld stub, a 63-76 mm tube, a 10 mm welded
   bottom, no bottom seal), with an internal shoulder that locates the sacrificial liner.
C. Glass rebuild: the stock plates, valve and tie rods with a fused-quartz tube in place of the
   borosilicate, FKM or silicone seals, and a stainless liner sleeve that covers the glass rim and the
   top seal.

Find precedents: published designs, manuals, theses, patents or incident reports for powder
collection canisters, cans or cyclones under metal atomizers (gas, ultrasonic, centrifugal, plasma),
especially how they are protected from unatomized molten metal, shot or splats, what materials and
seals they use, whether they have isolation valves, how they are cooled or instrumented, and any
failures where hot metal reached the collection container, melted seals or cracked glass. Include
lab-scale and university-built atomizers. Give citations with DOIs or URLs.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Integration of circular economy principles into additive manufacturing (AM) has emerged as a critical strategy for addressing economic and environmental challenges associated with the high-cost, resource-intensive production of NiTi shape memory alloys (SMAs). This review presents a comprehensive analysis of the ultrasonic plasma atomization (UPA) technique as an advanced recycling approach for converting NiTi AM waste into high-quality feedstock. Furthermore, UPA demonstrates significant potential as a dual-function method, enabling both alloying and fine powder production within a single integrated process. AM processes, such as powder bed fusion-laser beam (PBF-LB), binder jetting, and direct energy deposition (DED), often result in substantial material losses, exacerbated by powder degradation phenomena including oxidation, particle morphology changes, and loss of flowability. While conventional atomization techniques, such as gas and plasma atomization, offer partial solutions for powder production, they are limited by significant energy inefficiencies, high capital investment requirements, and increased risks of contamination. Moreover, powders produced via gas atomization typically exhibit inferior quality compared to those generated by UPA, including lower sphericity and a higher prevalence of surface satellites. In contrast, the UPA system, a hybrid technique combining high-frequency ultrasonic vibrations and plasma melting, offers precise control over droplet formation through acoustic cavitation, Faraday wave instabilities, and rapid solidification, enabling the production of highly spherical, homogeneous, and contamination-minimized NiTi powders. Drawing on thermofluidic principles, vibrational mechanics, and metallurgical kinetics, this review systematically deconstructs the UPA mechanism, highlighting key phenomena such as resonance-induced cavitation dynamics, ultrasonic capillary wave collapse, and non-equilibrium solidification. Furthermore, it investigates contamination pathways specific to UPA and proposes strategies for impurity mitigation, including sonotrode design optimization, inert atmosphere refinement, and post-atomization conditioning. Experimental findings are analyzed to demonstrate the feasibility of achieving high sphericity (> 0.9), compositionally stable, and thermally responsive NiTi powders from recycled feedstock. Finally, the review outlines a roadmap for industrial-scale deployment, advocating the integration of machine learning and closed-loop recycling models to enhance process predictability, quality control, and resource efficiency. The insights presented herein position UPA as a transformative solution for enabling sustainable, high-performance NiTi powder regeneration within AM workflows, advancing the circular economy in advanced manufacturing.</jats:p>

Abstract:
The article presents the results of the development works and research on the atomization process carried out using two prototype high-power ultrasonic systems. Ultrasonic systems have been designed to develop a new metal powder production process; these materials are increasingly used in modern manufacturing processes such as additive technologies or spraying and surfacing processes. The preliminary studies presented in the article were conducted for water to assess the effectiveness of both systems and to verify the theoretical and structural assumptions. In ultrasonic atomization, the ultrasonic wave causes the phenomenon of cavitation, which leads to the overcoming of the surface tension forces of the liquid and its disintegration into fine droplets. The important parameters that affect the properties of the produced droplets include, among others, the frequency of the sonotrode vibrations and the amplitude of the vibrations of the working plate. As part of the research, the paper presents the process of selecting the sonotrode geometry for two different values of the transducer’s natural frequencies (20 kHz and 70 kHz). In the design process, the finite element method was used to perform a harmonic analysis and develop the geometry of the sonotrode and the working plate. The design assumptions and the design process were presented. The modeled and then ultrasonic waveguides were verified experimentally by measuring the deflection distribution on the working plate surface using a high-precision laser displacement sensor. Then, the work ultimately resulted in conducting atomization tests of water. The obtained aerosols and the mechanism of their formation were studied using a high-speed camera. Finally, using Matlab R2020a software and image analysis scripts, it was possible to analyze the droplet size distribution generated by both systems. It was observed that 50% of the produced droplets were in the range of 35–55 μm for a 20 kHz system, while for a 70 kHz system it was 10–25 μm, which is a very satisfying distribution in terms of metal powder atomization.

A new powder production method has been developed to speed up the search for novel alloys for additive manufacturing. The technique involves an ultrasonically agitated cold crucible installed at the top of a 20 kHz ultrasonic sonotrode. The material is melted with an electric arc and undergoes pulverization with standing wave vibrations. Several different alloys in various forms, including noble and metallic glass alloys, were chosen to test the process. The innovative ultrasonic atomization method appears as a promising tool for material scientists to develop powders with tailored chemical composition, size and structure.

Abstract:
Ultrasonic melt processing (UMP) has garnered significant attention from both academic and industrial communities as a promising solution to critical challenges in the metal casting industry. This technique offers a clean, environmentally friendly, and energy-efficient approach to improving melt quality and achieving structural refinement. However, due to the opaque nature of metals, understanding the fundamental mechanisms governing the interactions among ultrasonic bubbles, acoustic streaming, and the melt remains still challenging. This review traces the evolution of UMP research, from its inception in the mid-20th century to recent advancements, with particular emphasis on the application of state-of-the-art synchrotron X-ray imaging and computational modeling. These approaches have been instrumental in unraveling the complex, multiscale dynamics occurring across both temporal and spatial scales. Key findings in various metallic alloy systems are critically reviewed, focusing on new insights into cavitation bubbles, acoustic streaming, and the interactions of growing solid phases in different alloys. Additionally, the review discusses the resulting phenomena, including grain refinement, fragmentation, and the mitigation of solidification defects, in detail. The review concludes by identifying critical research gaps and emerging trends, underscoring the indispensable role of in situ studies and robust theoretical frameworks in advancing UMP. These developments are poised to reshape the future of innovation in materials science and engineering.

This review focuses on the current state of the art in liquid metal additive manufacturing (AM), an emerging and growing family of related printing technologies used to fabricate near-net shape or fully free-standing metal objects. The various printing modes and droplet generation techniques as applied to liquid metals are discussed. Two different printing modes, continuous and drop-on-demand (DOD), exist for liquid metal printing and are based on commercial inkjet printing technology. Several techniques are in various stages of development from laboratory testing, prototyping, to full commercialization. Printing techniques include metal droplet generation by piezoelectric actuation or impact-driven, electrostatic, pneumatic, electrohydrodynamic (EHD), magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) ejection, or droplet generation by application of a high-power laser. The impetus for development of liquid metal printing was the precise, and often small scale, jetting of solder alloys for microelectronics applications. The fabrication of higher-melting-point metals and alloys and the printing of free-standing metal objects has provided further motivation for the research and development of liquid metal printing.

Abstract:
As a 0D material, powder particles can be used to create almost any complicated engineering component by utilizing the high‐performance manufacturing capabilities of additive manufacturing (AM). Although powder‐based AM methods provide an outstanding practical value and development for modern manufacturing world, they continue to face challenges such as a lack of accessible categories, temperature restrictions, and poor performance of molded components. Therefore, researching for new AM materials and procedures has become an extremely necessary endeavor. For this purpose, a firm grasp of the current state of the art of powder‐based AM technologies is imperative. Hence, herein, a comprehensive review is presented on the most widely used powder‐based AM methods, and the materials used by these methods. For each method, the development and current state, operating principles, limitations, and future prospects are summarized. In contrast, for materials, their classifications, properties, and preparation methods are explored in great detail, while also commenting on the specific compatibilities between powder materials and powder methods. Industrial and commercialized applications of powder‐based AM are also presented in this work. Finally, the limitations of the current powder‐based technologies are highlighted, with comments regarding the future of this field.

Abstract:
<jats:p>High-quality Fe-Cr-Ni-W-B spherical powder is crucial for the powder metallurgy preparation of high-strength and tough Fe-Cr-Ni-W-B alloys. In this study, the controlled preparation of high-quality Fe-Cr-Ni-W-B spherical powder was achieved using the vacuum gas atomization method. The effects and mechanisms of atomization gas pressure, the melt nozzle inner diameter, and heat treatment temperature on the microstructure and flowability of Fe-Cr-Ni-W-B spherical powder were systematically investigated. By optimizing process parameters, spherical Fe-Cr-Ni-W-B powder with a sphericity of 95.1% and a flowability of 15.88 s/50 g was obtained, laying the foundation for the powder metallurgy preparation of high-strength and tough Fe-Cr-Ni-W-B alloys.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Metallic powders for additive manufacturing (AM) processes are primarily produced by gas atomization, which consists of three steps: melting, atomization and cooling. In the present work, we report on the refurbishing of a laboratory-scale gas atomizer. The equipment facilitates small-scale atomization, useful for developing powders tailored specifically to metal AM processes (e.g. binder jetting, laser powder-bed fusion and direct energy deposition). The refurbished atomizer is operated by an in-house measurement and control system, fully equipped with pressure, oxygen, gas-flow and temperature sensors that allow the user to experiment with the input parameters, and thus, understand how they affect the physical and chemical properties of powders. In this paper, the working principle of the laboratory-scale gas atomizer is presented and the main characteristics of the newly refurbished equipment are described.

Abstract:
Additive manufacturing (AM) has been intensively studied over this decade due to the increasing demand of functional and precise materials in various industries. AM process leverages on the concept of layer by layer deposition or joining of a material at micro‐ or nano‐scale to produce the final products. As such, AM technology is widely used to manufacture products of complex geometries with high precision in a short time. As the quality and the performance of AM manufactured functional products depend on the quality and the cost of the atomized metal or alloy powder used, the use of powders of high size uniformity, high purity, high sphericity, high flowability, low cost, and no trapped gas bubble porosity is necessary. To this end, various metal production technologies were investigated and one of the popular technologies is atomization. This article reviewed the working principles of the various atomization technologies for the production of fine metal and alloy powders. The key atomization conditions discussed in this article include atomization type, material feed rate and temperature, atomizing fluid flow rate, type and temperature, cooling rate, and atomization pressure. In addition, several outlooks on the prospect and the optimization of atomization technologies were also discussed in this article.

Abstract:
Gas atomization is one of the methods for production of clean metal powders at relatively moderate cost. A laboratory scale gas atomizer was designed and fabricated indigenously to produce metal powders with a batch capacity of 500g of copper (Cu). The design includes several features regarding fabrication and operation to provide optimum conditions for atomization. The inner diameter of atomizing chamber is 440 mm and its height is 1200 mm. The atomizing nozzle is of annular confined convergent type with an angle of 25o . Argon gas at desired pressure has been used for atomizing the metals to produce relatively clean powders. A provision has also been made to view the atomization process. The indigenous laboratory scale gas atomizer was used to produce tin (Sn) and copper (Cu) powders with different atomizing gas pressures ranging from 2 to 10 bar. The particle size of different powders produced ranges from 40 to 400 Âµm.

From text 'khan2010developmentofindigenous pages 2-4'.

K. K. Khan, A. M. Qasim, and P. Ahmed. Development of indigenous laboratory scale gas atomizer for producing metal powders. The Nucleus, 48:51-56, Dec 2010. URL: https://doi.org/10.71330/thenucleus.2011.866, doi:10.71330/thenucleus.2011.866. This article has 1 citations.

Khan et al. (2010), pp. 52–53, explicitly describe the powder-collection system. Following atomization, the gas–powder stream enters a stainless-steel, conical cyclone separator tangentially, producing cyclonic flow that separates solids from gas. Powder settles into a stainless-steel powder collector, while gas exits through the cyclone’s circulation line and is returned to the chamber as a shower through connections in the supporting lid. The assembly also includes a relief valve to discharge excess gas and prevent over-pressure; a pressure gauge on the cylindrical atomizing chamber provides pressure monitoring. For process sensing, the molten copper temperature is measured with a K-type thermocouple (p. 52), and the chamber includes a viewport for observing atomization. The documented atomization failure mechanism is freezing of molten metal inside the teeming nozzle, identified as dependent on nozzle design; the paper also notes that dangerous melt ejection can result from positive pressure at the metal exit, which the circulation-line aspiration effect is intended to prevent (p. 53). This excerpt provides no explicit construction or operation details for metal splash traps, isolating valves, or water cooling. It also does not document a separate collection canister or collection cone beyond the cyclone and stainless-steel powder collector. Claims about those features, or about the other cited publications, cannot be supported by this excerpt.

## pqac-00000001

From text 'potts2017developmentofa pages 39-46'.

CW Potts. Development of a centrifugal atomizer. Unknown journal, 2017.

Potts 2017 explicitly describes a centrifugal atomizer’s collection arrangement as a collection funnel at the bottom of the atomizing chamber. The funnel receives powder after it has cooled in the chamber; the excerpt does not describe a separate collection canister, cone geometry beyond the funnel, cyclone, metal-splash trap, or isolating valve. It states that liquid nitrogen may sometimes be placed at the bottom to protect collected powder from surface oxidation. The chamber atmosphere is controlled through a gas inlet and vacuum outlet, typically using nitrogen or argon to reduce contamination and oxidation. Water cooling is specified for the induction coil because induced temperatures could melt the copper coil; the high-speed motor also requires sufficient cooling because of high rotational speeds and conducted heat. Temperature sensing and control use an infrared thermocouple, PID controller, solid-state relay, and induction-driver system. Explicitly documented failure or hazard modes include nozzle cooling that prevents melt flow from the crucible, possible copper-coil melting without water cooling, oxidation or contamination, and heat transmission to the motor spindle. These points are documented in the excerpt (approximately pp. 29–30). Any inference about splash containment, cyclone separation, valve isolation, or vessel failure would be speculation rather than stated evidence.

From text 'hohmann1990modernsystemsfor pages 2-3'.

M. Hohmann and S. Jönsson. Modern systems for production of high quality metal alloy powder. Vacuum, 41:2173-2176, Jan 1990. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/0042-207x(90)94217-e, doi:10.1016/0042-207x(90)94217-e. This article has 16 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt provides explicit information chiefly about powder collection, cyclone separation, and cooling in inert-gas atomization systems. Atomization-gas exhaust is located at the lower cylindrical section of the tower and incorporates a cyclone to separate fine particles carried by the gas. The product is normally recovered as coarse and fine fractions, which are mixed before classification to maximize yield. For production-scale systems, the tower’s lower end is recommended to connect to pneumatic conveying: atomized particles are transported by the gas into a cyclone separator, allowing collection of the complete product in one container. The same conveying line permits cooling by introducing additional cooling gas. These passages document a cyclone, a collection container, pneumatic transport, and gas-based cooling; they do not explicitly describe a collection cone, metal splash traps, isolating valves, sensors, or failure modes of the atomization collection apparatus. Separately, the melting section states that molten material is collected in a water-cooled copper crucible and maintained liquid with additional heating before atomization. The excerpt also discusses operational risks in guided-stream jet systems, including increased thermal stress in ceramic parts and greater operational risk from process-parameter variation, but this is not identified as a collection-vessel failure.

The del Rio et al. 2022 excerpt provides documented construction and operation details for the powder-collection path and instrumentation, but not for every component named in the question. After atomization, powder is collected in a bottom-mounted powder container. A cyclone is installed between the atomization chamber and this container; it removes gas and large particles, with the gas vented to atmosphere and large particles collected in a water filter. The powder container is sealed and handled in a glovebox to prevent contamination, and later sieving can provide selected particle-size ranges. The excerpt does not explicitly describe a collection cone, metal-splash traps, isolating valves, or a water-cooling system. The “water filter” is documented as a collection device for large particles, but should not be interpreted as water cooling. Instrumentation includes zirconium-oxide oxygen sensors in both melting and atomization chambers, chamber pressure transducers, gas-flow measurement, nozzle-pressure measurement, thermocouples, and an optical pyrometer. Oxygen is continuously recorded, and atomization starts only below 0.1% O2. The excerpt discusses process control and particle cooling, including convection and radiation, but reports no atomization failures. M Hohmann  and S J6nsson,  Leybold AG, D-6450 Hanau, FRG





The production of components for high temperature and high strength applications requires clean metal
powder of high tap density. One of the leading technologies for the production of such powders  is the
inert-gas atomization of metal alloy melts. Around the world these powders  will be produced with a standard
type of inert-gas atomizer equipped with an induction or vacuum induction furnace. Recently a new type of
vacuum induction furnace was developed by Leybold which opens the possiblity for cleaner products and the
multi-use of one big furnace for different applications, e.g. the combination of an atomizer together with a
continous casting station. This combined application of a high quality vacuum induction furnace makes the
investment of such systems less risky and increases the quality of the material production. A further step
toward the production of cleaner materials is the application of cold crucible techniques mainly in connection
with plasma heat sources. Today this technique, together with inert-gas atomization, starts to become a
commerical process for the production of ultraclean and titanium alloy powder.

and O2 in the powder is important. For our experiments, the S content is analyzed in the material before
melting by the infrared absorption method after combustion in an induction furnace (LECO Analyzer).
Same measurement is performed for the atomized powder. The O2 content in the melt and powder is
affected by the atmosphere in both the melting and atomization chambers. Zirconium oxide flow-based
O2 sensors are  installed (A19-P Angst+Pfister). One sensor  is located in each chamber with a
measurement range between 1 and 1000 ppm and a resolution of 1 ppm. The sensor locations are shown
in figure 1b. Low O2 concentrations are achieved by two means: Initially, a 0.01 mbar absolute pressure
in the equipment is attained by pumping. Subsequently, a non-reactive gas is used to fill the chambers
and to create an inert atmosphere, usually N2 or Ar, which helps in dissipating O2. In the described
system, N2 is used. The O2 levels are measured and recorded during the whole atomization process. We
use the oxygen concentration as a conditional limit for starting the atomization process. The program is
set to start only if the O2 levels are below 0.1%.
   The mass flow rate ratio between the molten metal and the gas, 𝐽𝑚𝑒𝑙𝑡𝐽𝑔𝑎𝑠⁄       , can be adjusted in the
system either by using a different atomizer and nozzle design or by increasing the gas pressure. The
latter will also affect the velocity of the atomizing gas, 𝑣𝑔𝑎𝑠.
   The two commonly used atomizer designs are free-fall and confined/close-coupled design (figure 3).
It is possible to obtain higher yields in small-to-medium sized particles (20–60 µm). By using a confined
design, 𝑑50 will be smaller as 𝐽𝑚𝑒𝑙𝑡𝐽𝑔𝑎𝑠⁄      is reduced since the gas velocity at the interaction with the
metal stream is maximized. The equipment is currently using the confined design. However, a free-fall
configuration could be attained by changing crucible. This is possible thanks to the modular approach

flow meter that uses the thermal mass flow measurement principle for calculating the gas entering the

atomization. The pressure at the gas nozzle is measured by a pressure transducer positioned at the nozzle.
The gas used to fill the melting and atomization chambers comes from the gas battery. The N2 pressure
at the melting chamber is controlled using a PID electronic pressure valve that regulates the gas supplied
to the chamber. It contains a proportional valve with a flow restrictor that allows the user to set different
N2 partial pressures during melting. The overpressure is controlled by a back pressure regulator system
that enables release of N2 from the melting chamber and maintain the set point.

   Pressure transducers are installed at each chamber; readings are collected and displayed by the
control program during the entire process. Several thermocouples are mounted including one inside the
stopper rod (alumina tube that prevents the melt to flow down to the atomization chamber before a pre-
defined temperature  is reached) so the melt temperature  is known at any time. Additional melt
temperature measurements are taken with an optical pyrometer located at the top of the melting chamber.
   Another relevant parameter in the atomization process, is the melt superheat. Melt superheat
influences the determination of the powder particle size as the melt surface tension, 𝜎0, is affected by
the melt temperature [16]. During solidification, cooling rate, solidification time and nucleation are
affected by the superheat in the metal droplet. The melt temperature is controlled in the process at the
induction furnace (50 kW power unit), where the power and heating time are defined. The thermocouple
located inside the stopper rod is continuously measuring the melt temperature so atomization is done
when the predefined superheat is achieved. By being able to adjust the solidification of the particles, the
powder microstructure can be tailored.

during the droplet trajectory before being collected at the powder container. The heat from the spherical

pressure of 2.5 bar could be reached inside the chambers. The process time for the complete process
depends on the material to be produced, for 316L stainless steel, the process time is around 90 min.
Once the atomization process is completed, the powder is collected in the powder container at the bottom
of the atomizer (figure 1a). A cyclone is located between the atomization chamber and the powder
container so the gas and big particles are removed. The gas is released to the atmosphere and the big
particles are collected in the water filter. The powder container is sealed and handled inside a glovebox
to avoid any contamination. Further categorization may be performed by sieving to obtain specific
particle size ranges.

3. Conclusions
A lab-scale vacuum induction gas atomization facility was refurbished with the purpose of having full
control over the atomizing parameters. The sensors and actuators installed allow the users to control and
acquire data from the main parameters that influence powder quality. Establishing stable atomization
conditions is a key facto

Abstract:
One of the concepts behind Generation IV reactors is a molten salt coolant system, where the materials for the reactor itself and for the primary and secondary circuit components are subjected to extreme chemical and thermal stresses. Due to the unavailability of these materials, a nickel–molybdenum alloy known as MoNiCr has been developed in the Czech Republic. This paper discusses the manufacturing process for the MoNiCr alloy, covering conventional casting technology, forming, powder atomization, additive manufacturing (AM) using the directed energy deposition (DED-LB) process, and final heat treatment. Special attention was given to the quality of the input powders for additive manufacturing, particularly regarding the optimization of the chemical composition, which significantly influenced the quality of the additively manufactured components. AM enables the realization of complex structural designs that are critical for energy applications, despite the high susceptibility of the MoNiCr alloy to solidification cracking. Through AM, a test body was successfully produced with a maximum defect rate of 0.03% and the following mechanical properties: a yield strength (YS) of 279 MPa, an ultimate tensile strength (UTS) of 602 MPa, and an elongation (El) of 51%.

Abstract:
In this study a material model is developed to predict the solidification microstructure of an additive-manufactured, fully dense magnesium (Mg) alloy using uniform droplet spraying (UDS). Specifically, the crystallite size distribution is simulated by a solidification model, consisting of a nucleation/fragmentation and a constrained growth description, calibrated via microstructural data from a single droplet splat. This is enabled by a semi-analytical thermal modeling framework, based on the superposition of moving Green’s and Rosenthal functions for the temperature field generated by a Gaussian source distribution. The model is implemented for layered ellipsoidal deposit sections on planar substrates by multi-pass spraying, and its predictions are validated against measured crystal sizes by image analysis of experimental micrographs of a Mg97ZnY2 alloy, to an error margin of ± 15%. The computationally efficient simulation provides insights to the deposit microstructure, and is intended as a process observer in a closed-loop, adaptive control scheme based on infrared temperature measurements.

    For gas atomization, in general, there is a large disadvantage with mass-production runs

    due to the excessive amount of heat that must be removed to cool the particles. The

    problem arises from being in a closed environment where the atmosphere is a gas that

    does not absorb heat very well and cannot transfer out enough heat to run for extended

    periods of time [32]. Therefore gas atomization is done in plants that produce typically

     less than 10,000 tons per year of powders [4].



    General precautions must be taken with gas atomization due to the formation of satellite

    thermal spray powders. These are super fine (2-10 microns) particles stuck to the surface

    of the coarser powders that free themselves during the final stages of cooling [4]. For

    materials like aluminum, these smaller particles can cause concern due to the reactivity of

    aluminum particles on such a small scale. Methods like vacuum pouring and utilizing

     large tundishes (5 ton) are common but costly, methods to reduce satellite particles from

    forming [4].



3.3 PLASMA ATOMIZATION

   The pursuit of more spheroidal powders has left engineers to create unique and more

     consistent machines capable of producing perfect powders with a higher tolerance in                                                                      25


sizing. The goal of plasma atomization is to appeal to higher melting temperature alloys

like Titanium and to generate particles on the scale of 50 microns or less. Powders of

these sizes are desired to be used in industry as fully densified powders for product

creation [33].



Plasma atomization is the process of using plasma jets in a similar orientation to that of a

closed-couple gas atomizer. The plasma jets convene into an apex and the material to be

melted passes through the apex and is converted to spheroidal powders [33]. Figure 3.4

gives an example of a plasma-arc production method for creating atomized particles. The

diagram shows a finely tuned electrode that is spun at thousands of rotations per minute

(RPM) to facilitate centrifugal forces to help break up the molten metal from the tip of

the electrode [34].





                    Figure 3.4: Plasma jet atomization of a rotating electrode.                                                                         26


    Most plasma jets are created using argon and hydrogen mixture to create extreme

    temperatures over 5813K (5540C) to 16923K (16650C) [34]. Plasma atomization, in this

     case, helps reduce contaminations from the chance of the material oxidizing or being

    introduced to foreign object contamination from alternating processes through a system.

   By the electrode being consumable and not multiple materials being put through a

    crucible like most atomization processes, it is easier to control the purity of the resulting

    powder [34]. Experiments carried out with titanium, and this method produced powders

     that were 67% within a consistent 14-20 microns [34]. The process may not give the

    highest yields but offers a novel way to overcome the higher melting alloys that could not

    be done, or was difficult with other techniques.



3.4 CENTRIFUGAL ATOMIZATION

    This section will be covered in much greater detail than other methods previously

    discussed since this process is the embodiment of the thesis and creates the necessary

    background to understand the terminology and process.



    Centrifugal atomization can be referred to produce powders of the coarsest size when

    compared to other methods [35]. The foundation for a centrifugal atomizer is using an

    induction heating system to melt and alloy and then extrude or gravity feed the melt

    through a constant diameter nozzle to a chamber where a constant atmosphere is

    maintained. Once the melt reaches the end of the nozzle is free falls to a rotating disk that

    has a specified geometry and uses the centrifugal forces to cause the melt to break off                                                                      27


into coarse particles and solidify in the atmosphere of the chamber. Once the material

solidifies, it falls to the bottom where it is collected and the sieved to size or post

processed to the desired qualities. Figure 3.6 is a conceptual two-dimensional (2D) model

of the core format for a centrifugal atomizer.





 Figure 3.5: Centrifugal atomization of steel at 70 kg min-1. Image courtesy of Woodhead Publishing
                                       Limited, 2013 [4].                                                                      28





                          Figure 3.6: Centrifugal atomizing chamber.
The centrifugal atomizer consists of ten principal components: (1) Fixture for holding

induction system and infrared thermocouple, (2) water-cooled induction coil and

insulated crucible, (3) graphite nozzle, (4) proportional-integral-derivate (PID) controller

and induction heater driver, (5) atomizing chamber, (6) atomizer disk or cup, (7) high

speed motor, (8) gas inlet, (9) vacuum outlet, (10) collection funnel. Some optional parts

of the machine include a nozzle that can cool or preheat the atomizer disk, or an inert gas

assisted entry nozzle to accelerate the melt into the chamber that increases smaller

particle consolidation.                                                                      29


The fixture for holding the induction is a sealed system typically that is attached to the

chamber in the same controlled atmosphere to prevent contamination. The water-cooled

induction coil heats the material contained within the crucible. Water cooling is required

to avoid melting the copper coil due to the induced temperatures. A simple water pump

can provide enough cooling fluid through the coil to prevent any such damage. The

graphite nozzle is what typically controls the entire melt flow. By having a different

diameter hole through the nozzle, the flow rate can be consistently controlled. Issues arise

with this method if the nozzle cools enough to where the metal cannot flow out of the

crucible. The PID controller and induction heater driver is a blanket statement for a

control system used to accurately monitor the temperature of the metal that is to be

melted. The PID controller uses feedback from typically an infrared (IR) thermocouple to

monitor the temperatures and to then send a digital I/O signal to a solid state relay that

controls power to the induction driver. The atomizing chamber is where the powder is

allowed to solidify and form. Typical centrifuges range from 2-3m in diameter to allow

sufficient space for particles to cool for large production plants. However, smaller

diameter centrifuges will be explored to test viability in smaller batch parameters. The

atomizer disk is one of the most researched components of a centrifugal atomizer due to

geometry having a significant role in the outcome of the powders formed. Atomizer disks

can sometimes have fins to help redirect the melt and wet the disc better, and the

atomizer cups can contribute to keeping particle size more consistent with the melt being

forced out of orifices on the side walls of the atomizing cup. The high-speed motor needs

to have sufficient cooling due to the high RPMs and the extreme temperatures that can                                                                      30


conduct through the atomizer through to the spindle. Speeds range from 2,000 RPMs to

30,000 RPMs and sometimes higher. The gas inlet and vacuum outlet are for controlling

the internal conditions of the chamber to make for consistent atmospheric conditions for

powder formation. It is typical to have an inert atmosphere of nitrogen or argon to detract

from contaminants and oxidation reactions as much as possible. The collection funnel is

where all the powder is collected after cooling in the chamber. Sometimes the bottom is

filled with a liquid gas like nitrogen to protect the powder from any surface oxidation.

However, this is not always done for every application.

droplet formation, (ii) ligament disintegration, and (iii) sheet disintegration [36]. These

three modes of particulate formation are what govern the final net shape that the particles

will take once they break away from the atomizer disk. An image was taken from Dr.

                       CHAPTER 4

           MODELING OF CENTRIFUGAL ATOMIZATION

Arguably the most exciting part of this research is the modeling of the centrifugal

atomization process. The complexity that is involved with the fluid dynamics and the

different dynamic forces enacted upon the liquid metal that sheer it off into atomized

particles make this of an interesting research topic. Beyond the modeling of the

atomization process is creating the boundary conditions that must surround the rotational

disk and melt. With these boundary conditions, the effort made to build a machine can be

carried out. Therefore, the purpose of this section is to give an overview of the different

modeling techniques that have been used, are used, and prove faithful to develop an

understanding of the centrifugal atomization process. The order in which this will be

discussed will be as follows: (i) an overview of the dynamics of particle formation and

the modes of disintegration, (ii) advanced computational fluid dynamics, (iii) the trial and

error of results and their discovery.                                                                      34

When the assembly was withdrawn, the lower broken stopper-rod section remained lodged in the nozzle throat, blocking liquid discharge and effectively plugging the nozzle. ## 1. mcwilliams2020failureanalysisof pages 1-4 (Context ID: pqac-00000028)
