function.arguments:
{"answer": "# Powder-collector precedents for the rePOWDER failure

**The closest published protection against the reported failure is a separate catch can *upstream* of the normal powder collector.** In an Ames Laboratory magnesium atomizer, the researchers suspended a can near the bottom of the chamber specifically to catch metal if the melt descended as a stream rather than atomizing. They also investigated an oil bath because large particles might still be liquid on reaching the chamber bottom and form splats. These are direct precedents for treating gross melt arrival as a design case, not merely for choosing a hotter-rated receiver seal. Steinmetz, *Investigation of a Novel Passivation Technique for Gas Atomized Magnesium Powders* (2011), https://doi.org/10.31274/etd-180810-3181. (pqac-00000059, pqac-00000060)

The following comparison separates documented hardware from features not disclosed in the sources. A collector that works after normal atomization is **not**, on that evidence alone, qualified to receive a substantially unatomized 816 g bronze charge.

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

## Findings most relevant to the proposed replacement

**Intercept hot shot before it reaches the receiver mouth.** The Ames catching can is the strongest experimentally described analogue to a sacrificial catch feature. A published *ultrasonic* atomization patent instead proposes a water-cooled chamber ending in a cone with a periodically opening baffle between cone and collector. Its drawing and description establish a possible separation architecture, but not that the baffle can stop a molten charge or that the patented device has been built and tested. WO2025060171A1, https://patents.google.com/patent/WO2025060171A1/en. Neither source establishes that an ordinary thin sleeve at the receiver entrance will prevent hot bronze from accumulating on its lip or conducting heat into the upper joint. (pqac-00000060, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023)

**Metal collectors and upstream cooling have precedents; their exact receiver seals usually do not.** A roughly 500 g copper-capacity university gas atomizer uses a stainless chamber, cyclone and stainless powder collector, plus a chamber pressure gauge and relief valve. Another laboratory atomizer seals its powder container after cyclone separation and handles it in a glovebox; it records chamber pressures, oxygen, gas flow and temperatures. An ATO Lab+ ultrasonic study reports water-jacketed chamber walls and cyclone cooling before powder settles into a promptly sealed container. None of these reports specifies a hot-shot-rated receiver O-ring, a sacrificial puck, or an approved KF clamp pressure rating. Khan *et al.*, *The Nucleus* (2011), https://doi.org/10.71330/thenucleus.2011.866; del Rio *et al.*, *IOP Conference Series: Materials Science and Engineering* (2022), https://doi.org/10.1088/1757-899X/1249/1/012034; Wróbel *et al.* (2026), https://doi.org/10.1007/s00170-026-18599-0. (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000021)

**An isolation valve has a documented purpose, but its position and seat exposure matter.** Hohmann and Jönsson describe a collection cone closed at its *lower end* by a valve so the connected powder container can be changed without losing the tower’s inert atmosphere. This supports including isolation when required for handling; it does **not** show that the present EPDM flap, or the proposed full-port ball valve, survives partly molten shot. A plasma-processing apparatus also uses a ball valve before stainless collection containers, but deliberately quenches powder into water, making it a poor dry-receiver thermal analogue. Hohmann and Jönsson, *Vacuum* (1990), https://doi.org/10.1016/0042-207X(90)94217-E; Khor, *Journal of Materials Processing Technology* (1992), https://doi.org/10.1016/0924-0136(92)90441-T. (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000014)

**Instrumentation should address the process as well as the vessel.** An outside-flange thermocouple can warn of conducted heating, but it measures neither the temperature of a pile at the entrance nor whether atomization has ceased. The Ames work shielded in-chamber thermocouples from falling metal and recorded chamber gas temperatures; del Rio *et al.* measured oxygen, pressure, gas flow and melt temperature. A separate documented gas-atomizer failure began with misleading melt thermocouple readings and excessive heating that broke ceramic components; the authors selected optical pyrometry as a corrective measure. Thus, the proposed flange alarms are supplementary rather than demonstrated protection against the fast-arriving shot described here. Steinmetz (2011), https://doi.org/10.31274/etd-180810-3181; del Rio *et al.* (2022), https://doi.org/10.1088/1757-899X/1249/1/012034; McWilliams *et al.*, *Journal of Failure Analysis and Prevention* (2020), https://doi.org/10.1007/s11668-020-00887-w. (pqac-00000060, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029)

## Assessment of A–C against the evidence

- **A — catalogue KF nipple and blank:** Removing the glass and the process-facing flap seat removes two components damaged in this run; a removable liner and bottom catch piece are plausible *proposed* sacrificial measures. However, no located atomizer publication validates this particular DN40–50 nipple, clamp, centring ring, FKM seal, liner or puck under a kilogram-scale hot-shot upset. The bottom blank leaves a second potentially hot joint. Verify the **actual mating flange standard**—KF and sanitary clamp parts are not interchangeable—and obtain assembly-specific ratings for full external-pressure evacuation, positive pressure through the relief setting, temperature and supported hanging load. A pressure-relief setting alone does not certify the receiver joint. The rationale for an upstream catch rather than relying only on a receiver liner follows the Ames experiment. (pqac-00000059, pqac-00000060)
- **B — welded metal vessel:** An integral bottom eliminates A’s bottom O-ring from the location of a hot pile and is consequently the more direct containment response to the described bottom-seal damage. Its weld, bottom, top flange and clamp still require design review and testing for the machine’s pressure/vacuum cycle and credible thermal upset. Stainless construction is precedented; the particular 10 mm bottom and 63–76 mm geometry are **not literature-validated specifications**. (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000063)
- **C — quartz glass rebuild:** Quartz has greater high-temperature capability than borosilicate, but it does not make the glass-to-plate seals, EPDM valve seat, or hot entrance safe. A vacuum-engineering thesis describes quartz for high-temperature use while cautioning that glass is brittle and poorly suited to mechanical loading; its material property is not a qualification for a clamped receiver exposed to impact and steep local temperature gradients. A sleeve that covers the rim must actually prevent direct shot contact and keep every seal below its compound-specific service temperature. On the evidence available, C retains more of the observed failure path than either metal concept. Rißlegger, *Design and Construction of an Acetylene Capable PVD Based Deposition System* (2020), https://doi.org/10.34726/hss.2020.67941. (pqac-00000041)

Replacing EPDM with **FKM or silicone is not a substitute for thermal separation**. Trelleborg’s reference tables give typical standard-compound upper operating temperatures of 130–150 °C for EPDM, 175 °C for silicone VMQ and 200 °C for FKM. The guide explicitly says actual allowable temperatures depend on the compound, medium and loading; none approaches direct contact with bronze poured at approximately 1300 °C. Trelleborg Sealing Solutions, *O-Rings and Back-up Rings*, technical guide, https://www.tss.trelleborg.com/. (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000050)

## Failure evidence and limits

Published failures confirm that atomization hardware can depart sharply from its normal thermal trajectory: in a calcium centrifugal atomizer the mild-steel disk separated about 10 seconds into a run, while melt continued atomizing on its ceramic support; the authors discuss splashing, skull formation and uneven thermal stress. At Ames, bonded stopper/pour-tube components could lift and drop a melt assembly, cracking the pour tube and allowing molten-material leakage. Neither paper reports a burned collector seal or cracked glass receiver. Tian *et al.*, *Powder Technology* (2017), https://doi.org/10.1016/j.powtec.2016.12.011; [name redacted] *et al.*, *Plasma Sprayed Pour Tubes and Other Melt Handling Components for Use in Gas Atomization* (2011), described in the retrieved Ames manuscript; McWilliams *et al.* (2020), https://doi.org/10.1007/s11668-020-00887-w. (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000061, pqac-00000062, pqac-00000029)

**No independently verifiable published report of hot metal reaching an atomizer’s glass collection tube and burning its elastomer seals was located.** The November 13 event in the question is therefore the direct evidence for that *specific* failure sequence; the cited studies establish relevant catch-can designs, cooling and isolation arrangements, and adjacent failure modes—not a previously reported identical incident. Likewise, no accessible rePOWDER manual verified the construction or performance of its proprietary cone shields or the manufacturer’s simple stainless cup. Those details, and the exact flange standard, remain to be confirmed against the machine and manufacturer rather than inferred from another atomizer. (pqac-00000059, pqac-00000060, pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000032)"}

{"answer": "# Powder-collector precedents for the rePOWDER failure

**The closest published protection against the reported failure is a separate catch can *upstream* of the normal powder collector.** In an Ames Laboratory magnesium atomizer, the researchers suspended a can near the bottom of the chamber specifically to catch metal if the melt descended as a stream rather than atomizing. They also investigated an oil bath because large particles might still be liquid on reaching the chamber bottom and form splats. These are direct precedents for treating gross melt arrival as a design case, not merely for choosing a hotter-rated receiver seal. Steinmetz, *Investigation of a Novel Passivation Technique for Gas Atomized Magnesium Powders* (2011), https://doi.org/10.31274/etd-180810-3181. (pqac-00000059, pqac-00000060)

The following comparison separates documented hardware from features not disclosed in the sources. A collector that works after normal atomization is **not**, on that evidence alone, qualified to receive a substantially unatomized 816 g bronze charge.

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

## Findings most relevant to the proposed replacement

**Intercept hot shot before it reaches the receiver mouth.** The Ames catching can is the strongest experimentally described analogue to a sacrificial catch feature. A published *ultrasonic* atomization patent instead proposes a water-cooled chamber ending in a cone with a periodically opening baffle between cone and collector. Its drawing and description establish a possible separation architecture, but not that the baffle can stop a molten charge or that the patented device has been built and tested. WO2025060171A1, https://patents.google.com/patent/WO2025060171A1/en. Neither source establishes that an ordinary thin sleeve at the receiver entrance will prevent hot bronze from accumulating on its lip or conducting heat into the upper joint. (pqac-00000060, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023)

**Metal collectors and upstream cooling have precedents; their exact receiver seals usually do not.** A roughly 500 g copper-capacity university gas atomizer uses a stainless chamber, cyclone and stainless powder collector, plus a chamber pressure gauge and relief valve. Another laboratory atomizer seals its powder container after cyclone separation and handles it in a glovebox; it records chamber pressures, oxygen, gas flow and temperatures. An ATO Lab+ ultrasonic study reports water-jacketed chamber walls and cyclone cooling before powder settles into a promptly sealed container. None of these reports specifies a hot-shot-rated receiver O-ring, a sacrificial puck, or an approved KF clamp pressure rating. Khan *et al.*, *The Nucleus* (2011), https://doi.org/10.71330/thenucleus.2011.866; del Rio *et al.*, *IOP Conference Series: Materials Science and Engineering* (2022), https://doi.org/10.1088/1757-899X/1249/1/012034; Wróbel *et al.* (2026), https://doi.org/10.1007/s00170-026-18599-0. (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000021)

**An isolation valve has a documented purpose, but its position and seat exposure matter.** Hohmann and Jönsson describe a collection cone closed at its *lower end* by a valve so the connected powder container can be changed without losing the tower’s inert atmosphere. This supports including isolation when required for handling; it does **not** show that the present EPDM flap, or the proposed full-port ball valve, survives partly molten shot. A plasma-processing apparatus also uses a ball valve before stainless collection containers, but deliberately quenches powder into water, making it a poor dry-receiver thermal analogue. Hohmann and Jönsson, *Vacuum* (1990), https://doi.org/10.1016/0042-207X(90)94217-E; Khor, *Journal of Materials Processing Technology* (1992), https://doi.org/10.1016/0924-0136(92)90441-T. (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000014)

The Ames work shielded in-chamber thermocouples from falling metal and recorded chamber gas temperatures; del Rio *et al.* measured oxygen, pressure, gas flow and melt temperature. A separate documented gas-atomizer failure began with misleading melt thermocouple readings and excessive heating that broke ceramic components; the authors selected optical pyrometry as a corrective measure. Thus, the proposed flange alarms are supplementary rather than demonstrated protection against the fast-arriving shot described here. Steinmetz (2011), https://doi.org/10.31274/etd-180810-3181; del Rio *et al.* (2022), https://doi.org/10.1088/1757-899X/1249/1/012034; McWilliams *et al.*, *Journal of Failure Analysis and Prevention* (2020), https://doi.org/10.1007/s11668-020-00887-w. (pqac-00000060, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029)

- **A — catalogue KF nipple and blank:** Removing the glass and the process-facing flap seat removes two components damaged in this run; a removable liner and bottom catch piece are plausible *proposed* sacrificial measures. However, no located atomizer publication validates this particular DN40–50 nipple, clamp, centring ring, FKM seal, liner or puck under a kilogram-scale hot-shot upset. The bottom blank leaves a second potentially hot joint. Verify the **actual mating flange standard**—KF and sanitary clamp parts are not interchangeable—and obtain assembly-specific ratings for full external-pressure evacuation, positive pressure through the relief setting, temperature and supported hanging load. A pressure-relief setting alone does not certify the receiver joint. The rationale for an upstream catch rather than relying only on a receiver liner follows the Ames experiment. (pqac-00000059, pqac-00000060)
- **B — welded metal vessel:** An integral bottom eliminates A’s bottom O-ring from the location of a hot pile and is consequently the more direct containment response to the described bottom-seal damage. Its weld, bottom, top flange and clamp still require design review and testing for the machine’s pressure/vacuum cycle and credible thermal upset. Stainless construction is precedented; the particular 10 mm bottom and 63–76 mm geometry are **not literature-validated specifications**. (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000063)

A sleeve that covers the rim must actually prevent direct shot contact and keep every seal below its compound-specific service temperature. On the evidence available, C retains more of the observed failure path than either metal concept. Trelleborg’s reference tables give typical standard-compound upper operating temperatures of 130–150 °C for EPDM, 175 °C for silicone VMQ and 200 °C for FKM. The guide explicitly says actual allowable temperatures depend on the compound, medium and loading; none approaches direct contact with bronze poured at approximately 1300 °C. Trelleborg Sealing Solutions, *O-Rings and Back-up Rings*, technical guide, https://www.tss.trelleborg.com/. (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000050)

(pqac-00000031, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000061, pqac-00000062, pqac-00000029)

Context. A university lab runs an AMAZEMET rePOWDER ultrasonic atomizer at about 1400 m altitude (room
pressure about 850-865 mbar). A 0.3-1.1 kg charge (aluminium alloys, and copper alloys such as
nickel-aluminium bronze UNS C63000 poured at about 1300 C) is induction-melted in a graphite crucible,
pushed through a 0.5 mm nozzle by argon over-pressure, and falls onto a plate vibrating at 40 kHz that
breaks it into powder (d50 roughly 100 um on good runs). Powder falls through a water-cooled stainless
cone under the chamber into a collection container that hangs from the cone's outlet flange on a
hinged clamp (ISO-KF style with a centring ring and O-ring, or possibly sanitary tri-clamp; size about
DN40-50, being confirmed). The chamber is evacuated to about 10 mbar absolute and backfilled with argon
several times, then runs at about +150 mbar gauge; a mechanical relief valve opens at +0.8 bar.
The stock container, top to bottom: the flange on a short neck, a conical reducer, a valve body with a
lever-operated flap valve whose seat is an EPDM ring, a borosilicate(?) glass tube about 100 mm across
in a perforated steel guard, sealed by elastomer rings in grooves of a top and a bottom stainless plate,
and four tie rods. A curved stainless splash plate sits in the bore at the top. The manufacturer also
supplies protective "shields" that fit in the cone; on the failed run they were not fitted and the
splash plate was in backwards.

The failure (Nov 13 2026): the plate barely atomized, so most of an 816 g C63000 charge left it as 1-3 mm
shot, still partly liquid when it reached the container about 0.4 s later. Bronze piled up at the
container's entrance; the glass glowed orange; the EPDM valve seat burned (white crust, smoke out of
the joint); the seals under the glass were damaged; the glass cracked at its top rim. Good runs never
damaged the container. The manufacturer says a "much simpler metal cup, without the glass" exists
(a stainless tube with a separate sanitary butterfly valve), and that in their own lab they mostly use
"the simple stainless steel" tube because it is easier to make and clean, but its delivery date is
unknown. The lab wants to build its own container within days to a few weeks, glass or metal.

The lab's design so far (to be reviewed, not assumed correct):
A. All-metal, catalogue parts only: a 316L ISO-KF full nipple (bore about 48 mm, 200-250 mm long) hung
   from the cone with the existing clamp; a KF blank flange at the bottom with a stainless centring ring
   and FKM O-ring; a drop-in 304/316 sacrificial liner sleeve in the top bore so that hot metal cannot
   touch the top O-ring; a loose copper or steel "catch puck" at the bottom to soak up heat and keep the
   pile off the bottom joint; Type K thermocouples clamped on the outside at the top flange and near the
   bottom, read by a panel meter with an alarm; no valve (a KF blank and clamp go on the top after
   removal), or a full-port valve whose seats are hidden behind the ball when open.
B. All-metal, turned and TIG-welded: one 316L vessel (KF weld stub, a 63-76 mm tube, a 10 mm welded
   bottom, no bottom seal), with an internal shoulder that locates the sacrificial liner.
C. Glass rebuild: the stock plates, valve and tie rods with a fused-quartz tube in place of the
   borosilicate, FKM or silicone seals, and a stainless liner sleeve that covers the glass rim and the
   top seal.

Find precedents: published designs, manuals, theses, patents or incident reports for powder
collection canisters, cans or cyclones under metal atomizers (gas, ultrasonic, centrifugal, plasma),
especially how they are protected from unatomized molten metal, shot or splats, what materials and
seals they use, whether they have isolation valves, how they are cooled or instrumented, and any
failures where hot metal reached the collection container, melted seals or cracked glass. Include
lab-scale and university-built atomizers. Give citations with DOIs or URLs.

contexts.context: Khan et al. (2010), pp. 52–53, explicitly describe the powder-collection system. Following atomization, the gas–powder stream enters a stainless-steel, conical cyclone separator tangentially, producing cyclonic flow that separates solids from gas. Powder settles into a stainless-steel powder collector, while gas exits through the cyclone’s circulation line and is returned to the chamber as a shower through connections in the supporting lid. The assembly also includes a relief valve to discharge excess gas and prevent over-pressure; a pressure gauge on the cylindrical atomizing chamber provides pressure monitoring. For process sensing, the molten copper temperature is measured with a K-type thermocouple (p. 52), and the chamber includes a viewport for observing atomization. The documented atomization failure mechanism is freezing of molten metal inside the teeming nozzle, identified as dependent on nozzle design; the paper also notes that dangerous melt ejection can result from positive pressure at the metal exit, which the circulation-line aspiration effect is intended to prevent (p. 53). This excerpt provides no explicit construction or operation details for metal splash traps, isolating valves, or water cooling. It also does not document a separate collection canister or collection cone beyond the cyclone and stainless-steel powder collector. Claims about those features, or about the other cited publications, cannot be supported by this excerpt.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes inert-gas atomization systems in which powder exits the lower atomization tower, with exhaust gas carrying fines to a cyclone; coarse and fine fractions are collected separately, or pneumatic conveying transports all powder to one container. Production systems may inject additional cooling gas into the conveying tube to cool product. Vertical gas atomization yields finer, narrower distributions than horizontal systems. Guided metal streams improve fine-powder efficiency but increase ceramic thermal stress and operational risk with high-melting charges. Molten-metal processing may use ceramic Al₂O₃/ZrO₂ foam filters (reported efficiencies 70–90%) and water-cooled copper crucibles.
contexts.question:
Context. A university lab runs an AMAZEMET rePOWDER ultrasonic atomizer at about 1400 m altitude (room
pressure about 850-865 mbar). A 0.3-1.1 kg charge (aluminium alloys, and copper alloys such as
nickel-aluminium bronze UNS C63000 poured at about 1300 C) is induction-melted in a graphite crucible,
pushed through a 0.5 mm nozzle by argon over-pressure, and falls onto a plate vibrating at 40 kHz that
breaks it into powder (d50 roughly 100 um on good runs). Powder falls through a water-cooled stainless
cone under the chamber into a collection container that hangs from the cone's outlet flange on a
hinged clamp (ISO-KF style with a centring ring and O-ring, or possibly sanitary tri-clamp; size about
DN40-50, being confirmed). The chamber is evacuated to about 10 mbar absolute and backfilled with argon
several times, then runs at about +150 mbar gauge; a mechanical relief valve opens at +0.8 bar.
The stock container, top to bottom: the flange on a short neck, a conical reducer, a valve body with a
lever-operated flap valve whose seat is an EPDM ring, a borosilicate(?) glass tube about 100 mm across
in a perforated steel guard, sealed by elastomer rings in grooves of a top and a bottom stainless plate,
and four tie rods. A curved stainless splash plate sits in the bore at the top. The manufacturer also
supplies protective "shields" that fit in the cone; on the failed run they were not fitted and the
splash plate was in backwards.

The failure (Nov 13 2026): the plate barely atomized, so most of an 816 g C63000 charge left it as 1-3 mm
shot, still partly liquid when it reached the container about 0.4 s later. Bronze piled up at the
container's entrance; the glass glowed orange; the EPDM valve seat burned (white crust, smoke out of
the joint); the seals under the glass were damaged; the glass cracked at its top rim. Good runs never
damaged the container. The manufacturer says a "much simpler metal cup, without the glass" exists
(a stainless tube with a separate sanitary butterfly valve), and that in their own lab they mostly use
"the simple stainless steel" tube because it is easier to make and clean, but its delivery date is
unknown. The lab wants to build its own container within days to a few weeks, glass or metal.

The lab's design so far (to be reviewed, not assumed correct):
A. All-metal, catalogue parts only: a 316L ISO-KF full nipple (bore about 48 mm, 200-250 mm long) hung
   from the cone with the existing clamp; a KF blank flange at the bottom with a stainless centring ring
   and FKM O-ring; a drop-in 304/316 sacrificial liner sleeve in the top bore so that hot metal cannot
   touch the top O-ring; a loose copper or steel "catch puck" at the bottom to soak up heat and keep the
   pile off the bottom joint; Type K thermocouples clamped on the outside at the top flange and near the
   bottom, read by a panel meter with an alarm; no valve (a KF blank and clamp go on the top after
   removal), or a full-port valve whose seats are hidden behind the ball when open.
B. All-metal, turned and TIG-welded: one 316L vessel (KF weld stub, a 63-76 mm tube, a 10 mm welded
   bottom, no bottom seal), with an internal shoulder that locates the sacrificial liner.
C. Glass rebuild: the stock plates, valve and tie rods with a fused-quartz tube in place of the
   borosilicate, FKM or silicone seals, and a stainless liner sleeve that covers the glass rim and the
   top seal.

Find precedents: published designs, manuals, theses, patents or incident reports for powder
collection canisters, cans or cyclones under metal atomizers (gas, ultrasonic, centrifugal, plasma),
especially how they are protected from unatomized molten metal, shot or splats, what materials and
seals they use, whether they have isolation valves, how they are cooled or instrumented, and any
failures where hot metal reached the collection container, melted seals or cracked glass. Include
lab-scale and university-built atomizers. Give citations with DOIs or URLs.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a university-built plasma micro-atomization system with a **water-cooled, double-wall stainless-steel chamber**, a 0–800°C thermocouple, tempered-glass viewing panel, and powder collection using **two filter bags clamped to stainless-steel containers** below the chamber. A rotating disk operates at **0–3000 rpm** (typical 900 rpm), with plasma-to-substrate distance **160 mm** and powder feed **20 g/min**. The system processed stainless steel 316 (melting point ~1450°C) and YSZ (~2200°C).

contexts.context: Ünal (Journal of Materials Processing Technology 180, 2006, pp. 291–295) describes a nitrogen gas atomizer using 1–3.5 MPa gas, a 10 kg stainless-steel tin crucible, and a 3 mm-ID alumina delivery tube. Its close-coupled nozzle has 20 convergent–divergent jets, 10.05 mm² throat area, 25° apex angle, and gas velocities approaching/exceeding Mach 2.5 (calculated Mach 3 at the divergent exit). Tip pressure was generally subambient, increasing suction and atomization stability; unstable pressure occurred with 10-mm tube protrusion. The excerpt provides no collector, seal, cooling, or hot-metal failure precedent.

contexts.context: A lab-scale vacuum induction gas atomizer uses a cyclone between the atomization chamber and powder container to remove gas and “big particles,” collecting oversize in a water filter; the sealed container is handled in a glovebox. The system uses N₂ or Ar after evacuation to 0.01 mbar, starts only below 0.1% O₂, and records chamber pressure, gas flow, melt temperature, and O₂ (1–1000 ppm sensors). It melts up to 10 kg and reaches 2.5 bar absolute. Droplet cooling is primarily convective—radiation is up to 100× smaller—with cooling governed by diameter and relative gas velocity. DOI: 10.1088/1757-899X/1249/1/012034.

contexts.context: The excerpt concerns AM powder flowability rather than atomizer collection hardware. It states that Van der Waals forces may provide “up to 80–90 % of inter-particle forces,” with finer powders more prone to agglomeration and poor flow. Hausner ratio (HR = tapped/bulk density) is commonly used: HR ≤ 1.25 indicates freely flowing powder, while cohesive/non-flowing powders typically have HR > 1.40. However, HR and ring-shear tests poorly represent dynamically spread, thin AM layers. Angle-of-repose/Hall-flow tests are closer to free discharge, though funnel size and operator filling can affect results.

contexts.context: Khan et al., “Development of indigenous laboratory scale gas atomizer,” *The Nucleus* 48 (2011), describes a ~500 g copper laboratory gas atomizer. Its 440 mm ID, 1200 mm tall stainless chamber feeds a stainless conical cyclone and stainless powder collector. The cyclone separates gas and particles, allowing droplets “enough time to solidify during their flight.” Design features include polished surfaces, a pressure gauge, K-type thermocouple, 0.5 mm annular nozzle, circulating gas/aspiration to prevent dangerous melt ejection, and a relief valve for over-pressure. The excerpt emphasizes preventing teeming-nozzle freezing and optimizing superheat.

nickel-aluminium bronze UNS C63000 poured at about 1300 C) is induction-melted in a graphite crucible,
pushed through a 0.5 mm nozzle by argon over-pressure, and falls onto a plate vibrating at 40 kHz that
breaks it into powder (d50 roughly 100 um on good runs). Powder falls through a water-cooled stainless
cone under the chamber into a collection container that hangs from the cone's outlet flange on a
hinged clamp (ISO-KF style with a centring ring and O-ring, or possibly sanitary tri-clamp; size about
DN40-50, being confirmed). The chamber is evacuated to about 10 mbar absolute and backfilled with argon
several times, then runs at about +150 mbar gauge; a mechanical relief valve opens at +0.8 bar.
The stock container, top to bottom: the flange on a short neck, a conical reducer, a valve body with a
lever-operated flap valve whose seat is an EPDM ring, a borosilicate(?) glass tube about 100 mm across
in a perforated steel guard, sealed by elastomer rings in grooves of a top and a bottom stainless plate,
and four tie rods. A curved stainless splash plate sits in the bore at the top. The manufacturer also
supplies protective "shields" that fit in the cone; on the failed run they were not fitted and the
splash plate was in backwards.

The failure (Nov 13 2026): the plate barely atomized, so most of an 816 g C63000 charge left it as 1-3 mm
shot, still partly liquid when it reached the container about 0.4 s later. Bronze piled up at the
container's entrance; the glass glowed orange; the EPDM valve seat burned (white crust, smoke out of
the joint); the seals under the glass were damaged; the glass cracked at its top rim. Good runs never
damaged the container. The manufacturer says a "much simpler metal cup, without the glass" exists
(a stainless tube with a separate sanitary butterfly valve), and that in their own lab they mostly use
"the simple stainless steel" tube because it is easier to make and clean, but its delivery date is
unknown. The lab wants to build its own container within days to a few weeks, glass or metal.

The lab's design so far (to be reviewed, not assumed correct):
A. All-metal, catalogue parts only: a 316L ISO-KF full nipple (bore about 48 mm, 200-250 mm long) hung
   from the cone with the existing clamp; a KF blank flange at the bottom with a stainless centring ring
   and FKM O-ring; a drop-in 304/316 sacrificial liner sleeve in the top bore so that hot metal cannot
   touch the top O-ring; a loose copper or steel "catch puck" at the bottom to soak up heat and keep the
   pile off the bottom joint; Type K thermocouples clamped on the outside at the top flange and near the
   bottom, read by a panel meter with an alarm; no valve (a KF blank and clamp go on the top after
   removal), or a full-port valve whose seats are hidden behind the ball when open.
B. All-metal, turned and TIG-welded: one 316L vessel (KF weld stub, a 63-76 mm tube, a 10 mm welded
   bottom, no bottom seal), with an internal shoulder that locates the sacrificial liner.
C. Glass rebuild: the stock plates, valve and tie rods with a fused-quartz tube in place of the
   borosilicate, FKM or silicone seals, and a stainless liner sleeve that covers the glass rim and the
   top seal.

Find precedents: published designs, manuals, theses, patents or incident reports for powder
collection canisters, cans or cyclones under metal atomizers (gas, ultrasonic, centrifugal, plasma),
especially how they are protected from unatomized molten metal, shot or splats, what materials and
seals they use, whether they have isolation valves, how they are cooled or instrumented, and any
failures where hot metal reached the collection container, melted seals or cracked glass. Include
lab-scale and university-built atomizers. Give citations with DOIs or URLs.

contexts.context: Hohmann and Jönsson describe inert-gas atomization as melting–atomization–solidification, emphasizing that melt temperature and mass-transfer rate strongly affect particle size and must remain uniform. Standard systems use induction or vacuum-induction furnaces; large nickel/cobalt/iron melts may be poured through a preheated ceramic tundish to limit heat loss and thermal mass. Graphite crucibles and stopper rods permit direct feeding to atomization. Cleaner production uses ceramic-free or cold-crucible methods; cold-crucible systems collect melt in a water-cooled copper crucible. No powder-collection-canister or hot-metal failure details are reported. (Vacuum/Volume 41, 1990, pp. 2173–2176.)

snippets: The process is carried out in an inert gas environment (typically argon 5.0), ensuring minimal contamination and oxidation.
The niobium wire, previously prepared via calibrated rolling, was mounted in the wire feeding system (WFS) and remained under an inert gas shield throughout the entire process to prevent oxidation.
The chamber was purged of residual gases by repeatedly applying vacuum cycles followed by argon backfilling, until an oxygen level below 200 ppm was reached.
Argon flow was maintained at 15 l/min to further reduce oxygen content below 10 ppm.
Argon also served additional roles: facilitating powder solidification and transport, as well as stabilizing the electric arc
Due to the appropriate selection of the atomization platform material, favorable wettability between niobium and the platform surface allowed the formation of a stable molten pool.

contexts.context: The Wróbel et al. (2026) excerpt describes powder collection within an ultrasonic niobium atomization system. After ejection, droplets entered an inert gas stream, where they cooled and solidified by convection and radiation. Further cooling occurred through contact with water-jacketed chamber walls and the cyclone. Aerodynamic forces directed particles toward the atomization-chamber outlet. The cyclone separated usable powder from ultrafine particles and process dust, after which the usable fraction settled by gravity into a collection container. The container was immediately sealed after processing to prevent post-process oxidation. The listed process parameters identify argon as the process gas, with an argon flow of 15 l/min and an oxygen level below 10 ppm; the shutdown sequence included stopping argon flow. contexts.context: The excerpt describes 3D Lab’s ATO Lab+ ultrasonic atomizer, a compact research-scale system for metals including high-melting niobium. It uses a selectable-frequency ultrasonic sonotrode (35 kHz in the study), inert argon, and an arc-melting platform. Experiments repeatedly evacuated/backfilled the chamber until oxygen was below 200 ppm, then maintained argon flow at 15 L/min to reduce oxygen below 10 ppm and aid powder solidification/transport. Niobium feed was 2.4 × 2.4 mm wire at 1.5 mm/s. The excerpt provides no collection-container design, shielding, seal, cooling, or failure information.
contexts.question:
Context. A university lab runs an AMAZEMET rePOWDER ultrasonic atomizer at about 1400 m altitude (room
pressure about 850-865 mbar). A 0.3-1.1 kg charge (aluminium alloys, and copper alloys such as
nickel-aluminium bronze UNS C63000 poured at about 1300 C) is induction-melted in a graphite crucible,
pushed through a 0.5 mm nozzle by argon over-pressure, and falls onto a plate vibrating at 40 kHz that
breaks it into powder (d50 roughly 100 um on good runs). Powder falls through a water-cooled stainless
cone under the chamber into a collection container that hangs from the cone's outlet flange on a
hinged clamp (ISO-KF style with a centring ring and O-ring, or possibly sanitary tri-clamp; size about
DN40-50, being confirmed). The chamber is evacuated to about 10 mbar absolute and backfilled with argon
several times, then runs at about +150 mbar gauge; a mechanical relief valve opens at +0.8 bar.
The stock container, top to bottom: the flange on a short neck, a conical reducer, a valve body with a
lever-operated flap valve whose seat is an EPDM ring, a borosilicate(?) glass tube about 100 mm across
in a perforated steel guard, sealed by elastomer rings in grooves of a top and a bottom stainless plate,
and four tie rods. A curved stainless splash plate sits in the bore at the top. The manufacturer also
supplies protective "shields" that fit in the cone; on the failed run they were not fitted and the
splash plate was in backwards.

The failure (Nov 13 2026): the plate barely atomized, so most of an 816 g C63000 charge left it as 1-3 mm
shot, still partly liquid when it reached the container about 0.4 s later. Bronze piled up at the
container's entrance; the glass glowed orange; the EPDM valve seat burned (white crust, smoke out of
the joint); the seals under the glass were damaged; the glass cracked at its top rim. Good runs never
damaged the container. The manufacturer says a "much simpler metal cup, without the glass" exists
(a stainless tube with a separate sanitary butterfly valve), and that in their own lab they mostly use
"the simple stainless steel" tube because it is easier to make and clean, but its delivery date is
unknown. The lab wants to build its own container within days to a few weeks, glass or metal.

The lab's design so far (to be reviewed, not assumed correct):
A. All-metal, catalogue parts only: a 316L ISO-KF full nipple (bore about 48 mm, 200-250 mm long) hung
   from the cone with the existing clamp; a KF blank flange at the bottom with a stainless centring ring
   and FKM O-ring; a drop-in 304/316 sacrificial liner sleeve in the top bore so that hot metal cannot
   touch the top O-ring; a loose copper or steel "catch puck" at the bottom to soak up heat and keep the
   pile off the bottom joint; Type K thermocouples clamped on the outside at the top flange and near the
   bottom, read by a panel meter with an alarm; no valve (a KF blank and clamp go on the top after
   removal), or a full-port valve whose seats are hidden behind the ball when open.
B. All-metal, turned and TIG-welded: one 316L vessel (KF weld stub, a 63-76 mm tube, a 10 mm welded
   bottom, no bottom seal), with an internal shoulder that locates the sacrificial liner.
C. Glass rebuild: the stock plates, valve and tie rods with a fused-quartz tube in place of the
   borosilicate, FKM or silicone seals, and a stainless liner sleeve that covers the glass rim and the
   top seal.

Find precedents: published designs, manuals, theses, patents or incident reports for powder
collection canisters, cans or cyclones under metal atomizers (gas, ultrasonic, centrifugal, plasma),
especially how they are protected from unatomized molten metal, shot or splats, what materials and
seals they use, whether they have isolation valves, how they are cooled or instrumented, and any
failures where hot metal reached the collection container, melted seals or cracked glass. Include
lab-scale and university-built atomizers. Give citations with DOIs or URLs.

It uses a water-cooled chamber wall maintained below 40°C, evacuation to ≤6.5×10⁻² Pa, then backfill to 10⁴–4×10⁴ Pa. Molten droplets are ultrasonically sputtered from a water-cooled copper crucible and contact the cooled chamber wall, solidifying into particles. The chamber narrows to a cone leading to a powder collector; an automatically opening baffle periodically releases accumulated powder into it. No collector material, seal, valve, thermal instrumentation, molten-metal failure, or incident details are reported. Claimed powder size is ≤60 μm.

contexts.context: The excerpt concerns centrifugal atomization, identifying three breakup modes: “direct droplet formation,” ligament disintegration, and sheet disintegration; disk wetting determines which occurs. It emphasizes modeling particle trajectories and cooling before container impact. For aluminum, listed properties include density 2.375 g/cm³, viscosity 0.005 Pa·s, surface tension 1.009 N/m, melting point 660.32°C, liquid temperature 800°C, disk radius 1 in, and air properties at room/800°C. Particle-size modeling uses a relation involving surface tension, density, angular speed, and radius. Assumptions include spherical, noninteracting droplets, no slip, and vertical-plane trajectories.

pushed through a 0.5 mm nozzle by argon over-pressure, and falls onto a plate vibrating at 40 kHz that
breaks it into powder (d50 roughly 100 um on good runs). Powder falls through a water-cooled stainless
cone under the chamber into a collection container that hangs from the cone's outlet flange on a
hinged clamp (ISO-KF style with a centring ring and O-ring, or possibly sanitary tri-clamp; size about
DN40-50, being confirmed). The chamber is evacuated to about 10 mbar absolute and backfilled with argon
several times, then runs at about +150 mbar gauge; a mechanical relief valve opens at +0.8 bar.
The stock container, top to bottom: the flange on a short neck, a conical reducer, a valve body with a
lever-operated flap valve whose seat is an EPDM ring, a borosilicate(?) glass tube about 100 mm across
in a perforated steel guard, sealed by elastomer rings in grooves of a top and a bottom stainless plate,
and four tie rods. A curved stainless splash plate sits in the bore at the top. The manufacturer also
supplies protective "shields" that fit in the cone; on the failed run they were not fitted and the
splash plate was in backwards.

shot, still partly liquid when it reached the container about 0.4 s later. Bronze piled up at the
container's entrance; the glass glowed orange; the EPDM valve seat burned (white crust, smoke out of
the joint); the seals under the glass were damaged; the glass cracked at its top rim. Good runs never
damaged the container. The manufacturer says a "much simpler metal cup, without the glass" exists
(a stainless tube with a separate sanitary butterfly valve), and that in their own lab they mostly use
"the simple stainless steel" tube because it is easier to make and clean, but its delivery date is
unknown. The lab wants to build its own container within days to a few weeks, glass or metal.

The lab's design so far (to be reviewed, not assumed correct):
A. All-metal, catalogue parts only: a 316L ISO-KF full nipple (bore about 48 mm, 200-250 mm long) hung
   from the cone with the existing clamp; a KF blank flange at the bottom with a stainless centring ring
   and FKM O-ring; a drop-in 304/316 sacrificial liner sleeve in the top bore so that hot metal cannot
   touch the top O-ring; a loose copper or steel "catch puck" at the bottom to soak up heat and keep the
   pile off the bottom joint; Type K thermocouples clamped on the outside at the top flange and near the
   bottom, read by a panel meter with an alarm; no valve (a KF blank and clamp go on the top after
   removal), or a full-port valve whose seats are hidden behind the ball when open.
B. All-metal, turned and TIG-welded: one 316L vessel (KF weld stub, a 63-76 mm tube, a 10 mm welded
   bottom, no bottom seal), with an internal shoulder that locates the sacrificial liner.
C. Glass rebuild: the stock plates, valve and tie rods with a fused-quartz tube in place of the
   borosilicate, FKM or silicone seals, and a stainless liner sleeve that covers the glass rim and the
   top seal.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes atomizer precedents relevant to collection design. Gas atomization has substantial heat-removal limitations in closed gas environments, and aluminum powders require precautions because 2–10 μm “satellite” particles may detach during cooling and are highly reactive. A centrifugal atomizer uses a controlled-atmosphere chamber, induction crucible, graphite nozzle, rotating disk/cup, gas/vacuum ports, and a bottom “collection funnel” where particles cool before collection; chambers may be 2–3 m in diameter. Optional disk cooling/preheating and inert-gas-assisted entry are noted. Collection may sometimes use liquid nitrogen to limit oxidation.

contexts.context: This excerpt documents McWilliams et al. (2020), DOI 10.1007/s11668-020-00887-w, and provides information on the gas atomizer’s materials, cooling arrangement, and catastrophic failure. The crucible was zirconia, the stopper rod was densified alumina, and thermocouples were housed in molybdenum sheaths inside alumina tubes with zirconia lids. After atomization, powder was collected in a cyclone separator; the excerpt does not identify the cyclone or collection-container material, nor does it describe a dedicated splash-prevention design or leak seals. Cooling was passive: the lower chamber supplied sufficient distance and time for powder to cool to a manageable handling temperature. The failure involved faulty thermocouple readings, excessive temperatures beyond the alumina components’ functional range, loss of thermocouples, failure of multiple ceramic components, and loss of the metal charge. The stopper rod did not extract because it fractured, with one or more ceramic pieces missing and the voids backfilled by liquid metal. A ceramic section also floated to the melt surface. The excerpt does not provide the requested Tian et al. 2017, Finotello, or Ciftci 2020 findings or their source DOIs.

contexts.context: The excerpt documents a catastrophic failure in a gas-spray atomization crucible during processing of a Pd alloy. The relevant ceramic components were an alumina stopper rod and thin-walled alumina thermocouple over-sheaths. Erroneous thermocouple readings caused excessive RF heating; the liquid-metal temperature was estimated at approximately 1,918–2,060 °C, near the alumina melting point of 2,072 °C. The authors conclude that alumina lost structural integrity at these temperatures. A mechanical load also contributed: a spring applied approximately 25.5 psi to the 0.5-inch stopper rod, while 1–3 mm misalignment produced a bending moment. The proposed mechanism was creep-rupture failure after the metal became liquid. The fractured stopper rod pieces and TC sheaths floated in the melt. When the assembly was withdrawn, the lower broken stopper-rod section remained lodged in the nozzle throat, blocking liquid discharge and effectively plugging the nozzle. The excerpt does not document a separate collection-container material, splash-prevention design, active cooling strategy, or leak seal. It instead identifies temperature-measurement/control failure and ceramic fracture as the principal hazards and states that infrared optical pyrometry was selected to replace thermocouples. Source DOI: 10.1007/s11668-020-00887-w. No findings for Tian et al. (2017), Finotello, or Ciftci (2020) are present in this excerpt.

contexts.context: The excerpt documents Tian et al.’s centrifugal atomizer with rotating quench bath (CARQB), but it does not identify the material of the collection container or bath. Collection uses a rotating quench bath, and the cited development history also mentions spray-quenching and liquid-borne collection. Splash prevention is addressed at the atomization disk: a cup-shaped profile pushes calcium against the disk to improve wetting, while a smooth surface prevents liquid splashing and produces an even melt film. Cooling and morphology control rely on the quench-bath system, inert chamber gas, and potentially high-thermal-conductivity helium to increase convective cooling and reduce secondary atomization. The design uses externally driven rotation and a ferrofluidic sealed feed-through, providing the excerpt’s explicit sealing detail. The chamber is vacuumed and backfilled with ultrahigh-purity inert gas at static positive pressure up to 34.5 kPa. The main documented failure hazard is skull detachment from the atomization disk, which could damage the device and degrade performance; skull formation also changes particle size and morphology. contexts.context: The Finotello, Verouden, and Thuy excerpt provides cooling-related findings for a gas atomizer but does not document a collection-container material, splash-prevention design, leak seals, or catastrophic failure. It states that most cooling occurs when the gas flow impinges on the molten-metal stream. Cooling depends significantly on the melt’s initial temperature, metal type, gas type, and gas temperature. The temperature differences between the droplet, gas, and atomization-chamber wall are identified as major determinants: larger differences between melt/droplet temperature and gas or wall temperature produce higher cooling rates, which accelerate droplet solidification. The excerpt reports an average gas-atomizer cooling rate of 10²–10³ K/s, attributed to variations in atomizer designs, metals, and gases. It also notes that convection and radiation are the two principal heat-transfer modes. The experimental water/air setup is described as having an air supply valve, pressure regulator, flow-control component, and an unavailable flow sensor; supplied air pressure was 0.3–0.5 MPa. These setup details do not establish splash protection, sealing, containment material, or failure behavior. No DOI is provided in the excerpt for the Finotello source, and the other named studies (Tian et al. 2017, McWilliams et al. 2020, and Ciftci 2020) are not included.

contexts.context: SRNL’s gas-atomization system used a steel vacuum chamber with a lower section providing sufficient distance/time for passively cooling powder before collection in a cyclone separator. It atomized metal through a nozzle using a 1,000-psi helium ring. The 100-kW induction system used zirconia crucibles, densified-alumina stopper rods, and Mo-sheathed C-type thermocouples inside alumina tubes. A 2,100-g charge was heated under argon. Thermocouple disagreement reached 312°C; faulty readings caused excessive temperatures, ceramic-component failure, and loss of the charge. X-ray/CT showed the stopper rod fractured and was backfilled by liquid metal.
contexts.question:
Context. A university lab runs an AMAZEMET rePOWDER ultrasonic atomizer at about 1400 m altitude (room
pressure about 850-865 mbar). A 0.3-1.1 kg charge (aluminium alloys, and copper alloys such as
nickel-aluminium bronze UNS C63000 poured at about 1300 C) is induction-melted in a graphite crucible,
pushed through a 0.5 mm nozzle by argon over-pressure, and falls onto a plate vibrating at 40 kHz that
breaks it into powder (d50 roughly 100 um on good runs). Powder falls through a water-cooled stainless
cone under the chamber into a collection container that hangs from the cone's outlet flange on a
hinged clamp (ISO-KF style with a centring ring and O-ring, or possibly sanitary tri-clamp; size about
DN40-50, being confirmed). The chamber is evacuated to about 10 mbar absolute and backfilled with argon
several times, then runs at about +150 mbar gauge; a mechanical relief valve opens at +0.8 bar.
The stock container, top to bottom: the flange on a short neck, a conical reducer, a valve body with a
lever-operated flap valve whose seat is an EPDM ring, a borosilicate(?) glass tube about 100 mm across
in a perforated steel guard, sealed by elastomer rings in grooves of a top and a bottom stainless plate,
and four tie rods. A curved stainless splash plate sits in the bore at the top. The manufacturer also
supplies protective "shields" that fit in the cone; on the failed run they were not fitted and the
splash plate was in backwards.

The failure (Nov 13 2026): the plate barely atomized, so most of an 816 g C63000 charge left it as 1-3 mm
shot, still partly liquid when it reached the container about 0.4 s later. Bronze piled up at the
container's entrance; the glass glowed orange; the EPDM valve seat burned (white crust, smoke out of
the joint); the seals under the glass were damaged; the glass cracked at its top rim. Good runs never
damaged the container. The manufacturer says a "much simpler metal cup, without the glass" exists
(a stainless tube with a separate sanitary butterfly valve), and that in their own lab they mostly use
"the simple stainless steel" tube because it is easier to make and clean, but its delivery date is
unknown. The lab wants to build its own container within days to a few weeks, glass or metal.

The lab's design so far (to be reviewed, not assumed correct):
A. All-metal, catalogue parts only: a 316L ISO-KF full nipple (bore about 48 mm, 200-250 mm long) hung
   from the cone with the existing clamp; a KF blank flange at the bottom with a stainless centring ring
   and FKM O-ring; a drop-in 304/316 sacrificial liner sleeve in the top bore so that hot metal cannot
   touch the top O-ring; a loose copper or steel "catch puck" at the bottom to soak up heat and keep the
   pile off the bottom joint; Type K thermocouples clamped on the outside at the top flange and near the
   bottom, read by a panel meter with an alarm; no valve (a KF blank and clamp go on the top after
   removal), or a full-port valve whose seats are hidden behind the ball when open.
B. All-metal, turned and TIG-welded: one 316L vessel (KF weld stub, a 63-76 mm tube, a 10 mm welded
   bottom, no bottom seal), with an internal shoulder that locates the sacrificial liner.
C. Glass rebuild: the stock plates, valve and tie rods with a fused-quartz tube in place of the
   borosilicate, FKM or silicone seals, and a stainless liner sleeve that covers the glass rim and the
   top seal.

Find precedents: published designs, manuals, theses, patents or incident reports for powder
collection canisters, cans or cyclones under metal atomizers (gas, ultrasonic, centrifugal, plasma),
especially how they are protected from unatomized molten metal, shot or splats, what materials and
seals they use, whether they have isolation valves, how they are cooled or instrumented, and any
failures where hot metal reached the collection container, melted seals or cracked glass. Include
lab-scale and university-built atomizers. Give citations with DOIs or URLs.

contexts.context: Tian et al. (Powder Technology 308, 2017, pp. 84–93) describe a CARQB calcium atomizer modeled on the 1993 Ames centrifugal atomizer (Osborne and Anderson). It used a mechanically pumped vacuum chamber, argon backfill/slight overpressure, a 51-mm cup-shaped low-carbon-steel disk on ceramic support, and a 1545-cm³ rotating oil quench bath (25-mm depth, ~150 rpm) designed to absorb heat from 300 g liquid Ca while minimizing particle impact. Ca was supplied through a crucible using 69 kPa argon head pressure. Unsealed openings allowed pre-stream dripping; solidified drips were cast off. The disk developed a skull and failed after ~10 s, though ceramic support completed atomization.

contexts.context: The excerpt compares metals for gas-atomizer design using Weber and Reynolds numbers. With 50 µm droplets, constant nitrogen properties and 600 m/s gas, Weber numbers were nearly identical (38.49–38.88), implying similar breakup, while Reynolds numbers ranged from 4,574.92 (titanium) to 16,881.09 (zinc), decreasing with melting point/viscosity and indicating less turbulent flow. Flow speeds were 3.82–6.75 m/s. It recommends further study with varying gas properties. The heating section discusses induction versus resistance heating, asserting induction has lower heat loss and faster melting but claiming it “only works for ferrous metals,” a potentially questionable statement for aluminium/copper.

contexts.context: A gas-spray atomization Pd-alloy incident documents overheating caused by erroneous thermocouple readings and excessive RF power. After melting at ~1,550°C, estimated metal temperature reached 1,918–2,060°C, near alumina’s 2,072°C melting point. Alumina TC sheaths and a ceramic stopper fractured; a 1–3 mm misalignment and ~25.5 psi spring load may have promoted creep rupture. Broken ceramic pieces floated in the melt, while the lower stopper fragment remained in the nozzle, plugging flow. The report recommends replacing contact thermocouples with infrared pyrometry. References include Lavernia-related gas-atomization studies and a 2016 review.

contexts.context: Tian et al. (Powder Technology 308, 2017, pp. 84–93) report a lab centrifugal Ca atomizer under Ar. A 50.8-mm disk rotating at 2094.4 rad/s processed 134.6 g in ~16 s (8.4 g/s); predicted regime was ligament disintegration (critical rates 1 and 18.9 g/s). Excessive melt impingement caused splashing, uneven liquid distribution, thermal stress, and failure of a mild-steel disk, leaving a solid Ca skull on the disk/ceramic. They attributed solidification partly to insufficient superheat and high ceramic heat capacity, proposing plasma-sprayed refractory metal (e.g., Ta). Resulting d50 values were 124–182 μm.

contexts.context: The excerpt concerns camera analysis of a water spray, not powder-collection hardware or molten-metal failures. PFV4 calibration covered a 110.570 × 55.285 mm field; recordings used 2 FPS, 1024×512 resolution, and 1/10,000 s shutter. Six frames were analyzed per pressure. The nozzle apex angle was 25°. Measured convergence angles decreased with pressure: at 0.3 MPa, α = 26.145° ± 2.114° and θ = 19.939° ± 1.383°; at 0.5 MPa, α = 19.404° ± 0.735° and θ = 16.051° ± 0.648°. Lighting caused major overexposure and asymmetric results; two opposing lamps were recommended.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes centrifugal atomizer precedents relevant to unatomized molten-metal hazards. Poor wetting or insufficient superheat forms a disk “skull,” which can detach and damage equipment; cup-shaped disks, roughness, coatings, preheating, and low-thermal-mass designs reduce buildup. Large droplets cool slowly and may remain liquid, striking chamber walls and producing splats through secondary atomization. Inert gas limits oxidation; helium improves convective cooling. A calcium system uses a heated cup-shaped steel/ceramic disk, argon pressure, and a rotating quench bath. Its chamber operates under static positive inert-gas pressure of ≤34.5 kPa; Ca is atomized at 20,000 rpm into 100–200 μm powder.

contexts.context: The excerpt states that borosilicate glass has relatively low thermal expansion and good thermal-shock resistance, while pure quartz (SiO₂) is used to approximately 1050 °C. Glass remains brittle with low tensile strength, limiting mechanically loaded components. Silicate ceramics operate up to about 1350 °C and alumina/pure oxides up to 1800 °C. Plastics are generally discouraged in vacuum due to low melting points, absorption, and permeation. Elastomers require consideration of temperature, permeability, outgassing, and chemical resistance; FKM/FPM/FFKM are preferred vacuum seals, usable in systems reaching roughly 10⁻⁸ mbar.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides general vacuum principles rather than atomizer-container precedents. Vacuum is pressure below 300 mbar (DIN 28400-1); pressure is \(p=F/A\), and ideal gas behavior follows \(pV=nRT=NkT\). Mean free path is \(\lambda=kT/(\sqrt{2}\pi d^2p)\), increasing as pressure decreases. Flow classification uses \(Kn=\lambda/d\): viscous for \(Kn<0.01\), transitional for \(0.01<Kn<1\), and molecular for \(Kn>1\), though boundaries vary. These relations could help assess gas flow and particle transport in evacuated/backfilled atomizer systems, but the excerpt discusses no materials, seals, cooling, collection cans, or failures.

contexts.context: The guide’s Table 3 gives FKM a normal operating temperature range of -20 to +200 °C (-4 to +392 °F), with special types extending the lower limit to -40 °C (-40 °F). FKM may be used for short periods up to +230 °C (+446 °F). For EPDM, peroxide-cured types are rated for normal operation from -45 to +150 °C (-49 to +302 °F), with short-period exposure up to +175 °C (+347 °F). Sulfur-cured EPDM types are rated from -45 to +130 °C (-49 to +266 °F), with short-period exposure up to +150 °C (+302 °F). The excerpt’s Figure 4 includes VMQ (silicone rubber) in the temperature-range comparison, but the supplied text does not provide a numeric VMQ range in a table; its plotted range should therefore be consulted directly in the original figure. The guide cautions that the illustrated temperature ranges apply only when the elastomer is used with compatible media. It also explains that media, oxygen, ozone, pressure, and temperature can alter material properties and sealing capability. FKM is associated with mineral oils and greases at high temperatures, while EPDM is commonly used with glycol-based brake fluids and hot water.

contexts.question:
Context. A university lab runs an AMAZEMET rePOWDER ultrasonic atomizer at about 1400 m altitude (room
pressure about 850-865 mbar). A 0.3-1.1 kg charge (aluminium alloys, and copper alloys such as
nickel-aluminium bronze UNS C63000 poured at about 1300 C) is induction-melted in a graphite crucible,
pushed through a 0.5 mm nozzle by argon over-pressure, and falls onto a plate vibrating at 40 kHz that
breaks it into powder (d50 roughly 100 um on good runs). Powder falls through a water-cooled stainless
cone under the chamber into a collection container that hangs from the cone's outlet flange on a
hinged clamp (ISO-KF style with a centring ring and O-ring, or possibly sanitary tri-clamp; size about
DN40-50, being confirmed). The chamber is evacuated to about 10 mbar absolute and backfilled with argon
several times, then runs at about +150 mbar gauge; a mechanical relief valve opens at +0.8 bar.
The stock container, top to bottom: the flange on a short neck, a conical reducer, a valve body with a
lever-operated flap valve whose seat is an EPDM ring, a borosilicate(?) glass tube about 100 mm across
in a perforated steel guard, sealed by elastomer rings in grooves of a top and a bottom stainless plate,
and four tie rods. A curved stainless splash plate sits in the bore at the top. The manufacturer also
supplies protective "shields" that fit in the cone; on the failed run they were not fitted and the
splash plate was in backwards.

The failure (Nov 13 2026): the plate barely atomized, so most of an 816 g C63000 charge left it as 1-3 mm
shot, still partly liquid when it reached the container about 0.4 s later. Bronze piled up at the
container's entrance; the glass glowed orange; the EPDM valve seat burned (white crust, smoke out of
the joint); the seals under the glass were damaged; the glass cracked at its top rim. Good runs never
damaged the container. The manufacturer says a "much simpler metal cup, without the glass" exists
(a stainless tube with a separate sanitary butterfly valve), and that in their own lab they mostly use
"the simple stainless steel" tube because it is easier to make and clean, but its delivery date is
unknown. The lab wants to build its own container within days to a few weeks, glass or metal.

The lab's design so far (to be reviewed, not assumed correct):
A. All-metal, catalogue parts only: a 316L ISO-KF full nipple (bore about 48 mm, 200-250 mm long) hung
   from the cone with the existing clamp; a KF blank flange at the bottom with a stainless centring ring
   and FKM O-ring; a drop-in 304/316 sacrificial liner sleeve in the top bore so that hot metal cannot
   touch the top O-ring; a loose copper or steel "catch puck" at the bottom to soak up heat and keep the
   pile off the bottom joint; Type K thermocouples clamped on the outside at the top flange and near the
   bottom, read by a panel meter with an alarm; no valve (a KF blank and clamp go on the top after
   removal), or a full-port valve whose seats are hidden behind the ball when open.
B. All-metal, turned and TIG-welded: one 316L vessel (KF weld stub, a 63-76 mm tube, a 10 mm welded
   bottom, no bottom seal), with an internal shoulder that locates the sacrificial liner.
C. Glass rebuild: the stock plates, valve and tie rods with a fused-quartz tube in place of the
   borosilicate, FKM or silicone seals, and a stainless liner sleeve that covers the glass rim and the
   top seal.

Find precedents: published designs, manuals, theses, patents or incident reports for powder
collection canisters, cans or cyclones under metal atomizers (gas, ultrasonic, centrifugal, plasma),
especially how they are protected from unatomized molten metal, shot or splats, what materials and
seals they use, whether they have isolation valves, how they are cooled or instrumented, and any
failures where hot metal reached the collection container, melted seals or cracked glass. Include
lab-scale and university-built atomizers. Give citations with DOIs or URLs.

contexts.context: The excerpt concerns a PVD gas-distribution/safety system rather than powder collection. It specifies elastomer-sealed MFCs, with EPDM selected because acetone from depleted acetylene cylinders can attack standard sealants. MFC flow is expressed in sccm, defined as gas volume at 0 °C and 1.013 bar. Safety relies on monitored valves, pressure, pumping, dilution, and flashback protection.

contexts.context: The excerpt documents the McWilliams et al. (2020) gas-spray atomization failure, but it does not report hot metal reaching the powder collection vessel, burning an elastomer O-ring, or cracking a glass receiver. The failed operation involved a Pd-alloy melt in the crucible: faulty thermocouple readings allowed temperatures to exceed the functional range of the alumina components, and the stopper rod failed to open the nozzle. After cooling, ceramic fragments were found at the surface of the frozen ingot, thermocouple sheath components had separated, and X-ray/CT imaging showed that the stopper rod had fractured with a substantial ceramic piece missing. The excerpt therefore supports McWilliams (2020) as a documented thermocouple/stopper-rod and ceramic-component failure, rather than as evidence of a collection-vessel incident. Tian (2017), including the reported disk-collapse event, is not included in this excerpt, so no details about that comparison can be verified here. On the supplied source text alone, the specific O-ring-burning or glass-receiver-cracking incident is absent.
contexts.question: Find any actual documented incident where hot metal reached powder collection vessel of a metal atomizer and burned elastomer O-ring, or cracked glass receiver. If absent say absent; identify documented closest component failures (Tian 2017 disk collapse and McWilliams 2020 thermocouple stopper). Search relevant source texts.

contexts.context: This excerpt does not document hot metal reaching a powder collection vessel, burning an elastomer O-ring, or cracking a glass receiver. It instead reports failures in the melt-delivery assembly caused by thermal bonding between the stopper rod and pour tube. When the bonded stopper was lifted, it could raise the entire melt system; after the bond released, the assembly could fall and crack components. The described sequence specifically includes a pour tube cracking mid-length and slipping past the insert edge, with the possibility of molten material leaking from the broken melt system. The resulting consequences included damage to the atomizer, costly repairs, and inability to initiate a run, sometimes requiring several days to tear down and re-equip the atomizer. The paper’s corrective measure was a three-layer composite stopper rod consisting of alumina, a tungsten reaction-barrier layer, and an outer yttria layer, intended to resist thermal bonding and melt attack. Subsequent testing found no apparent melt attack up to 1815°C, although some alumina/tungsten interface de-cohesion occurred. Thus, this source supplies a documented closest failure involving a cracked pour tube, stopper adhesion, assembly collapse, and potential molten leakage—not the requested collection-vessel/O-ring or glass-receiver incident. contexts.question:
Context. A university lab runs an AMAZEMET rePOWDER ultrasonic atomizer at about 1400 m altitude (room
pressure about 850-865 mbar). A 0.3-1.1 kg charge (aluminium alloys, and copper alloys such as
nickel-aluminium bronze UNS C63000 poured at about 1300 C) is induction-melted in a graphite crucible,
pushed through a 0.5 mm nozzle by argon over-pressure, and falls onto a plate vibrating at 40 kHz that
breaks it into powder (d50 roughly 100 um on good runs). Powder falls through a water-cooled stainless
cone under the chamber into a collection container that hangs from the cone's outlet flange on a
hinged clamp (ISO-KF style with a centring ring and O-ring, or possibly sanitary tri-clamp; size about
DN40-50, being confirmed). The chamber is evacuated to about 10 mbar absolute and backfilled with argon
several times, then runs at about +150 mbar gauge; a mechanical relief valve opens at +0.8 bar.
The stock container, top to bottom: the flange on a short neck, a conical reducer, a valve body with a
lever-operated flap valve whose seat is an EPDM ring, a borosilicate(?) glass tube about 100 mm across
in a perforated steel guard, sealed by elastomer rings in grooves of a top and a bottom stainless plate,
and four tie rods. A curved stainless splash plate sits in the bore at the top. The manufacturer also
supplies protective "shields" that fit in the cone; on the failed run they were not fitted and the
splash plate was in backwards.

The failure (Nov 13 2026): the plate barely atomized, so most of an 816 g C63000 charge left it as 1-3 mm
shot, still partly liquid when it reached the container about 0.4 s later. Bronze piled up at the
container's entrance; the glass glowed orange; the EPDM valve seat burned (white crust, smoke out of
the joint); the seals under the glass were damaged; the glass cracked at its top rim. Good runs never
damaged the container. The manufacturer says a "much simpler metal cup, without the glass" exists
(a stainless tube with a separate sanitary butterfly valve), and that in their own lab they mostly use
"the simple stainless steel" tube because it is easier to make and clean, but its delivery date is
unknown. The lab wants to build its own container within days to a few weeks, glass or metal.

The lab's design so far (to be reviewed, not assumed correct):
A. All-metal, catalogue parts only: a 316L ISO-KF full nipple (bore about 48 mm, 200-250 mm long) hung
   from the cone with the existing clamp; a KF blank flange at the bottom with a stainless centring ring
   and FKM O-ring; a drop-in 304/316 sacrificial liner sleeve in the top bore so that hot metal cannot
   touch the top O-ring; a loose copper or steel "catch puck" at the bottom to soak up heat and keep the
   pile off the bottom joint; Type K thermocouples clamped on the outside at the top flange and near the
   bottom, read by a panel meter with an alarm; no valve (a KF blank and clamp go on the top after
   removal), or a full-port valve whose seats are hidden behind the ball when open.
B. All-metal, turned and TIG-welded: one 316L vessel (KF weld stub, a 63-76 mm tube, a 10 mm welded
   bottom, no bottom seal), with an internal shoulder that locates the sacrificial liner.
C. Glass rebuild: the stock plates, valve and tie rods with a fused-quartz tube in place of the
   borosilicate, FKM or silicone seals, and a stainless liner sleeve that covers the glass rim and the
   top seal.

Find precedents: published designs, manuals, theses, patents or incident reports for powder
collection canisters, cans or cyclones under metal atomizers (gas, ultrasonic, centrifugal, plasma),
especially how they are protected from unatomized molten metal, shot or splats, what materials and
seals they use, whether they have isolation valves, how they are cooled or instrumented, and any
failures where hot metal reached the collection container, melted seals or cracked glass. Include
lab-scale and university-built atomizers. Give citations with DOIs or URLs.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a high-pressure argon gas atomizer evacuated below 400 milli-torr, with melt released through a graphite/alumina pour assembly. Powder was separated by a primary cyclone, secondary cyclone, then wet scrubber. In magnesium trials, a suspended “catching can” near the chamber bottom was specifically provided to intercept an unbroken metal stream. Type-K thermocouples were protected by beveled ¼-inch stainless-steel sleeves, which successfully prevented falling metal from covering most beads. Magnesium processing used a steel melt system, 667 g at 725 °C, ¼-inch orifice, and 70 psig atomization gas.

contexts.context: The excerpt concerns Ames Laboratory gas-atomizer melt-system failures, not collection cans. A stopper rod bonding to a pour tube can lift the entire melt assembly, which may crash down, crack the tube, and release molten material; recovery can require “several days.” Their solution used an Al₂O₃ tube with plasma-sprayed tungsten reaction barrier and external Y₂O₃, successfully used six times at temperatures up to 1815°C, with no melt attack. YSZ showed notable thermal-shock resistance. Tungsten also reduced thermocouple “noise.” Fabrication took about 3 hours and materials cost approximately $80 per 12-inch rod. References include [name redacted] et al. (2010) and patents US 6,358,466 and 6,425,504.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a thermal-plasma nanopowder/coating system using a 304 stainless-steel chamber, 460 mm diameter × 860 mm long, with 1.5 mm walls and a 5 mm water jacket. Its conical bottom connects to collectors: a first collector makes a 90° gas turn, retaining “relatively coarse” particles; a downstream cyclone makes a 180° turn, retaining finer particles. The cyclone uses a double-walled, water-cooled pipe, and aerosol then enters a powder-collection unit before a scroll pump. The excerpt provides no specific molten-metal impact, seal-failure, valve, or glass-protection incident.
