Question: Context. A university lab runs an AMAZEMET rePOWDER ultrasonic atomizer at about 1400 m altitude (room
pressure about 850-865 mbar). A 0.3-1.1 kg charge (aluminium alloys, and copper alloys such as
nickel-aluminium bronze UNS C63000 poured at about 1300 C) is induction-melted in a graphite crucible,
pushed through a 0.5 mm nozzle by argon over-pressure, and falls onto a plate vibrating at 40 kHz that
breaks it into powder (d50 roughly 100 um on good runs). Powder falls through a water-cooled stainless
cone under the chamber into a collection container that hangs from the cone's outlet flange on a
hinged clamp (ISO-KF style with a centring ring and O-ring, or possibly sanitary tri-clamp; size about
DN40-50, being confirmed). The chamber is evacuated to about 10 mbar absolute and backfilled with argon
several times, then runs at about +150 mbar gauge; a mechanical relief valve opens at +0.8 bar.
The stock container, top to bottom: the flange on a short neck, a conical reducer, a valve body with a
lever-operated flap valve whose seat is an EPDM ring, a borosilicate(?) glass tube about 100 mm across
in a perforated steel guard, sealed by elastomer rings in grooves of a top and a bottom stainless plate,
and four tie rods. A curved stainless splash plate sits in the bore at the top. The manufacturer also
supplies protective "shields" that fit in the cone; on the failed run they were not fitted and the
splash plate was in backwards.

The failure (Nov 13 2026): the plate barely atomized, so most of an 816 g C63000 charge left it as 1-3 mm
shot, still partly liquid when it reached the container about 0.4 s later. Bronze piled up at the
container's entrance; the glass glowed orange; the EPDM valve seat burned (white crust, smoke out of
the joint); the seals under the glass were damaged; the glass cracked at its top rim. Good runs never
damaged the container. The manufacturer says a "much simpler metal cup, without the glass" exists
(a stainless tube with a separate sanitary butterfly valve), and that in their own lab they mostly use
"the simple stainless steel" tube because it is easier to make and clean, but its delivery date is
unknown. The lab wants to build its own container within days to a few weeks, glass or metal.

The lab's design so far (to be reviewed, not assumed correct):
A. All-metal, catalogue parts only: a 316L ISO-KF full nipple (bore about 48 mm, 200-250 mm long) hung
   from the cone with the existing clamp; a KF blank flange at the bottom with a stainless centring ring
   and FKM O-ring; a drop-in 304/316 sacrificial liner sleeve in the top bore so that hot metal cannot
   touch the top O-ring; a loose copper or steel "catch puck" at the bottom to soak up heat and keep the
   pile off the bottom joint; Type K thermocouples clamped on the outside at the top flange and near the
   bottom, read by a panel meter with an alarm; no valve (a KF blank and clamp go on the top after
   removal), or a full-port valve whose seats are hidden behind the ball when open.
B. All-metal, turned and TIG-welded: one 316L vessel (KF weld stub, a 63-76 mm tube, a 10 mm welded
   bottom, no bottom seal), with an internal shoulder that locates the sacrificial liner.
C. Glass rebuild: the stock plates, valve and tie rods with a fused-quartz tube in place of the
   borosilicate, FKM or silicone seals, and a stainless liner sleeve that covers the glass rim and the
   top seal.

Find precedents: published designs, manuals, theses, patents or incident reports for powder
collection canisters, cans or cyclones under metal atomizers (gas, ultrasonic, centrifugal, plasma),
especially how they are protected from unatomized molten metal, shot or splats, what materials and
seals they use, whether they have isolation valves, how they are cooled or instrumented, and any
failures where hot metal reached the collection container, melted seals or cracked glass. Include
lab-scale and university-built atomizers. Give citations with DOIs or URLs.


Yes. # Powder-collector precedents for the rePOWDER failure

**The closest published protection against the reported failure is a separate catch can *upstream* of the normal powder collector.** In an Ames Laboratory magnesium atomizer, the researchers suspended a can near the bottom of the chamber specifically to catch metal if the melt descended as a stream rather than atomizing. They also investigated an oil bath because large particles might still be liquid on reaching the chamber bottom and form splats. These are direct precedents for treating gross melt arrival as a design case, not merely for choosing a hotter-rated receiver seal. Steinmetz, *Investigation of a Novel Passivation Technique for Gas Atomized Magnesium Powders* (2011), https://doi.org/10.31274/etd-180810-3181. (steinmetz2011investigationofa pages 38-42, steinmetz2011investigationofa pages 42-46)

The following comparison separates documented hardware from features not disclosed in the sources. A collector that works after normal atomization is **not**, on that evidence alone, qualified to receive a substantially unatomized 816 g bronze charge.

| Source and URL/DOI | Documented collector and controls | Transferability and limits |
|---|---|---|
| **Steinmetz (2011), Ames Laboratory Mg gas atomizer** — [DOI](https://doi.org/10.31274/etd-180810-3181) | A suspended metal **catching can** near the chamber bottom intercepted magnesium arriving as an unbroken stream. Normal product passed through paired funnels, two cyclones, and a wet scrubber. Gas curtains limited early wall impact; shielded thermocouples monitored the chamber. (steinmetz2011investigationofa pages 38-42, steinmetz2011investigationofa pages 42-46) | Strong direct precedent for an upstream sacrificial catch pot. The large gas-atomization tower differs substantially; can geometry, material grade, seals, and pressure rating are unspecified. |
| **Wróbel et al. (2026), ATO Lab+ ultrasonic atomizer** — [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00170-026-18599-0) | Droplets received additional cooling from **water-jacketed chamber walls and the cyclone**. The cyclone removed ultrafines and process dust; usable powder settled by gravity into a collection container that was sealed immediately after processing. Argon flow and oxygen were monitored. (wrobel2026enhancingniobiumpowder pages 2-5, wrobel2026enhancingniobiumpowder pages 5-7) | Direct small-batch ultrasonic precedent for cooling and separation before collection. Collector material, seal type, isolation valve, and protection against a gross unatomized stream are not disclosed. |
| **WO 2025/060171 A1, ultrasonic atomization patent** — [Google Patents](https://patents.google.com/patent/WO2025060171A1/en) | Proposed water-cooled vacuum chamber with a conical lower end. A **baffle at the collector connection opens automatically at intervals**, allowing accumulated powder to fall into the bottom collector; chamber-wall coolant outlet is specified below 40 °C. (WO2025060171A1 pages 4-6, WO2025060171A1 pages 6-9) | Closely relevant architecture: cooled cone plus an intervening barrier. This is a **patent proposal**, not demonstrated service or proof of resistance to a full molten charge; collector material and seals are unspecified. |
| **Hohmann and Jönsson (1990), industrial inert-gas atomization** — [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/0042-207X(90)94217-E) | The tower terminates in a powder-collection cone closed by a lower **isolation valve**, permitting replacement of the connected container without disturbing the inert atmosphere. Pneumatic transfer to a cyclone and single container, with optional cooling gas, is also described. (hohmann1990modernsystemsfor pages 2-3, hohmann1990modernsystemsfor pages 3-4) | Strong precedent for receiver isolation. Production-scale equipment; valve construction, seat material, splash resistance, seals, and pressure rating are not reported. |
| **Khan, Qasim and Ahmed (2011), university gas atomizer** — [DOI](https://doi.org/10.71330/thenucleus.2011.866) | A stainless-steel cylindrical/conical chamber feeds a stainless-steel cyclone and **stainless-steel powder collector**. A chamber pressure gauge and relief valve address overpressure; melt temperature is measured by a Type-K thermocouple. (khan2010developmentofindigenous pages 2-4) | Supports an all-metal collector and pressure monitoring for a roughly 500 g Cu research system. No collector isolation valve, liner, active collector cooling, seal material, or molten-stream trap is documented. |
| **del Rio et al. (2022), university laboratory gas atomizer** — [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1088/1757-899X/1249/1/012034) | A cyclone precedes the bottom powder container; gas vents to atmosphere and large particles enter a water filter. The container is **sealed and handled in a glovebox**. Instrumentation includes pressure transducers, oxygen sensors, gas-flow and nozzle-pressure measurement, thermocouples, and optical pyrometry. (rio2022laboratoryscalegasatomizer pages 4-6) | Good precedent for sealed handling and comprehensive sensing. The water filter is a separator, not documented collector cooling; container material, seals, isolation valve, and gross-melt protection are unspecified. |
| **Khor (1992), plasma melt and rapid-solidification apparatus** — [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/0924-0136(92)90441-T) | Double-wall stainless chamber with circulating cooling water and a 0–800 °C thermocouple. Water-quenched product passes through a ball valve into filter bags clamped to stainless-steel containers. (khor1992productionoffine pages 4-8) | Demonstrates water-jacketed stainless construction, temperature measurement, and valved collection, but it is an intentionally **wet quench/filter system**, not a dry inert receiver for partly molten bulk metal. |
| **Tian et al. (2017), Ames calcium centrifugal atomizer** — [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.powtec.2016.12.011) | A rotating bath containing 1,545 cm³ of mechanical-vacuum-pump oil quenched and collected particles; co-rotation reduced impact velocity and distributed heat. During a run, the mild-steel atomization disk failed after about 10 s; atomization continued on its ceramic support. (tian2017productionoffine pages 2-3, tian2017productionoffine pages 3-4, tian2017productionoffine pages 4-5, tian2017productionoffine media 26e3efc6) | Demonstrates deliberate thermal buffering and a real molten-metal component failure. Oil quenching creates contamination, fire, and compatibility issues and does not establish elastomer or glass receiver performance. |


*Table: Eight documented collection arrangements spanning ultrasonic, gas, plasma, and centrifugal atomizers. The comparison distinguishes demonstrated hardware from a patent proposal and identifies undisclosed seals, ratings, and melt-protection details.*

## Findings most relevant to the proposed replacement

**Intercept hot shot before it reaches the receiver mouth.** The Ames catching can is the strongest experimentally described analogue to a sacrificial catch feature. A published *ultrasonic* atomization patent instead proposes a water-cooled chamber ending in a cone with a periodically opening baffle between cone and collector. Its drawing and description establish a possible separation architecture, but not that the baffle can stop a molten charge or that the patented device has been built and tested. WO2025060171A1, https://patents.google.com/patent/WO2025060171A1/en. Neither source establishes that an ordinary thin sleeve at the receiver entrance will prevent hot bronze from accumulating on its lip or conducting heat into the upper joint. (steinmetz2011investigationofa pages 42-46, WO2025060171A1 pages 4-6, WO2025060171A1 pages 6-9)

**Metal collectors and upstream cooling have precedents; their exact receiver seals usually do not.** A roughly 500 g copper-capacity university gas atomizer uses a stainless chamber, cyclone and stainless powder collector, plus a chamber pressure gauge and relief valve. Another laboratory atomizer seals its powder container after cyclone separation and handles it in a glovebox; it records chamber pressures, oxygen, gas flow and temperatures. An ATO Lab+ ultrasonic study reports water-jacketed chamber walls and cyclone cooling before powder settles into a promptly sealed container. None of these reports specifies a hot-shot-rated receiver O-ring, a sacrificial puck, or an approved KF clamp pressure rating. Khan *et al.*, *The Nucleus* (2011), https://doi.org/10.71330/thenucleus.2011.866; del Rio *et al.*, *IOP Conference Series: Materials Science and Engineering* (2022), https://doi.org/10.1088/1757-899X/1249/1/012034; Wróbel *et al.* (2026), https://doi.org/10.1007/s00170-026-18599-0. (khan2010developmentofindigenous pages 2-4, rio2022laboratoryscalegasatomizer pages 4-6, wrobel2026enhancingniobiumpowder pages 5-7)

**An isolation valve has a documented purpose, but its position and seat exposure matter.** Hohmann and Jönsson describe a collection cone closed at its *lower end* by a valve so the connected powder container can be changed without losing the tower’s inert atmosphere. This supports including isolation when required for handling; it does **not** show that the present EPDM flap, or the proposed full-port ball valve, survives partly molten shot. A plasma-processing apparatus also uses a ball valve before stainless collection containers, but deliberately quenches powder into water, making it a poor dry-receiver thermal analogue. Hohmann and Jönsson, *Vacuum* (1990), https://doi.org/10.1016/0042-207X(90)94217-E; Khor, *Journal of Materials Processing Technology* (1992), https://doi.org/10.1016/0924-0136(92)90441-T. (hohmann1990modernsystemsfor pages 3-4, khor1992productionoffine pages 4-8)

**Instrumentation should address the process as well as the vessel.** An outside-flange thermocouple can warn of conducted heating, but it measures neither the temperature of a pile at the entrance nor whether atomization has ceased. The Ames work shielded in-chamber thermocouples from falling metal and recorded chamber gas temperatures; del Rio *et al.* measured oxygen, pressure, gas flow and melt temperature. A separate documented gas-atomizer failure began with misleading melt thermocouple readings and excessive heating that broke ceramic components; the authors selected optical pyrometry as a corrective measure. Thus, the proposed flange alarms are supplementary rather than demonstrated protection against the fast-arriving shot described here. Steinmetz (2011), https://doi.org/10.31274/etd-180810-3181; del Rio *et al.* (2022), https://doi.org/10.1088/1757-899X/1249/1/012034; McWilliams *et al.*, *Journal of Failure Analysis and Prevention* (2020), https://doi.org/10.1007/s11668-020-00887-w. (steinmetz2011investigationofa pages 42-46, rio2022laboratoryscalegasatomizer pages 4-6, mcwilliams2020failureanalysisof pages 1-4, mcwilliams2020failureanalysisof pages 4-10)

## Assessment of A–C against the evidence

- **A — catalogue KF nipple and blank:** Removing the glass and the process-facing flap seat removes two components damaged in this run; a removable liner and bottom catch piece are plausible *proposed* sacrificial measures. However, no located atomizer publication validates this particular DN40–50 nipple, clamp, centring ring, FKM seal, liner or puck under a kilogram-scale hot-shot upset. The bottom blank leaves a second potentially hot joint. Verify the **actual mating flange standard**—KF and sanitary clamp parts are not interchangeable—and obtain assembly-specific ratings for full external-pressure evacuation, positive pressure through the relief setting, temperature and supported hanging load. A pressure-relief setting alone does not certify the receiver joint. The rationale for an upstream catch rather than relying only on a receiver liner follows the Ames experiment. (steinmetz2011investigationofa pages 38-42, steinmetz2011investigationofa pages 42-46)
- **B — welded metal vessel:** An integral bottom eliminates A’s bottom O-ring from the location of a hot pile and is consequently the more direct containment response to the described bottom-seal damage. Its weld, bottom, top flange and clamp still require design review and testing for the machine’s pressure/vacuum cycle and credible thermal upset. Stainless construction is precedented; the particular 10 mm bottom and 63–76 mm geometry are **not literature-validated specifications**. (khan2010developmentofindigenous pages 2-4, yıldırım2017designandconstruction pages 44-52)
- **C — quartz glass rebuild:** Quartz has greater high-temperature capability than borosilicate, but it does not make the glass-to-plate seals, EPDM valve seat, or hot entrance safe. A vacuum-engineering thesis describes quartz for high-temperature use while cautioning that glass is brittle and poorly suited to mechanical loading; its material property is not a qualification for a clamped receiver exposed to impact and steep local temperature gradients. A sleeve that covers the rim must actually prevent direct shot contact and keep every seal below its compound-specific service temperature. On the evidence available, C retains more of the observed failure path than either metal concept. Rißlegger, *Design and Construction of an Acetylene Capable PVD Based Deposition System* (2020), https://doi.org/10.34726/hss.2020.67941. (risslegger2020designandconstruction pages 21-24)

Replacing EPDM with **FKM or silicone is not a substitute for thermal separation**. Trelleborg’s reference tables give typical standard-compound upper operating temperatures of 130–150 °C for EPDM, 175 °C for silicone VMQ and 200 °C for FKM. The guide explicitly says actual allowable temperatures depend on the compound, medium and loading; none approaches direct contact with bronze poured at approximately 1300 °C. Trelleborg Sealing Solutions, *O-Rings and Back-up Rings*, technical guide, https://www.tss.trelleborg.com/. (solutions2016oringsandbackup pages 43-45, solutions2016oringsandbackup pages 45-47)

## Failure evidence and limits

Published failures confirm that atomization hardware can depart sharply from its normal thermal trajectory: in a calcium centrifugal atomizer the mild-steel disk separated about 10 seconds into a run, while melt continued atomizing on its ceramic support; the authors discuss splashing, skull formation and uneven thermal stress. At Ames, bonded stopper/pour-tube components could lift and drop a melt assembly, cracking the pour tube and allowing molten-material leakage. Neither paper reports a burned collector seal or cracked glass receiver. Tian *et al.*, *Powder Technology* (2017), https://doi.org/10.1016/j.powtec.2016.12.011; [name redacted] *et al.*, *Plasma Sprayed Pour Tubes and Other Melt Handling Components for Use in Gas Atomization* (2011), described in the retrieved Ames manuscript; McWilliams *et al.* (2020), https://doi.org/10.1007/s11668-020-00887-w. (tian2017productionoffine pages 3-4, tian2017productionoffine pages 4-5, [name redacted]2011plasmasprayedpour pages 5-13, [name redacted]2011plasmasprayedpour pages 13-16, mcwilliams2020failureanalysisof pages 4-10)

**No independently verifiable published report of hot metal reaching an atomizer’s glass collection tube and burning its elastomer seals was located.** The November 13 event in the question is therefore the direct evidence for that *specific* failure sequence; the cited studies establish relevant catch-can designs, cooling and isolation arrangements, and adjacent failure modes—not a previously reported identical incident. Likewise, no accessible rePOWDER manual verified the construction or performance of its proprietary cone shields or the manufacturer’s simple stainless cup. Those details, and the exact flange standard, remain to be confirmed against the machine and manufacturer rather than inferred from another atomizer. (steinmetz2011investigationofa pages 38-42, steinmetz2011investigationofa pages 42-46, wrobel2026enhancingniobiumpowder pages 5-7, WO2025060171A1 pages 4-6, mcwilliams2020failureanalysisof pages 1-4, tian2017productionoffine pages 4-5)

The large gas-atomization tower differs substantially; can geometry, material grade, seals, and pressure rating are unspecified. |
| **Wróbel et al. (2026), ATO Lab+ ultrasonic atomizer** — [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00170-026-18599-0) | Droplets received additional cooling from **water-jacketed chamber walls and the cyclone**. The cyclone removed ultrafines and process dust; usable powder settled by gravity into a collection container that was sealed immediately after processing. Argon flow and oxygen were monitored. (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021) | Direct small-batch ultrasonic precedent for cooling and separation before collection. Collector material, seal type, isolation valve, and protection against a gross unatomized stream are not disclosed. |
| **WO 2025/060171 A1, ultrasonic atomization patent** — [Google Patents](https://patents.google.com/patent/WO2025060171A1/en) | Proposed water-cooled vacuum chamber with a conical lower end. A **baffle at the collector connection opens automatically at intervals**, allowing accumulated powder to fall into the bottom collector; chamber-wall coolant outlet is specified below 40 °C. (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023) | Closely relevant architecture: cooled cone plus an intervening barrier. This is a **patent proposal**, not demonstrated service or proof of resistance to a full molten charge; collector material and seals are unspecified. |
| **Hohmann and Jönsson (1990), industrial inert-gas atomization** — [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/0042-207X(90)94217-E) | The tower terminates in a powder-collection cone closed by a lower **isolation valve**, permitting replacement of the connected container without disturbing the inert atmosphere. Pneumatic transfer to a cyclone and single container, with optional cooling gas, is also described. (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011) | Strong precedent for receiver isolation. Production-scale equipment; valve construction, seat material, splash resistance, seals, and pressure rating are not reported. |
| **Khan, Qasim and Ahmed (2011), university gas atomizer** — [DOI](https://doi.org/10.71330/thenucleus.2011.866) | A stainless-steel cylindrical/conical chamber feeds a stainless-steel cyclone and **stainless-steel powder collector**. A chamber pressure gauge and relief valve address overpressure; melt temperature is measured by a Type-K thermocouple. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000015) | Supports an all-metal collector and pressure monitoring for a roughly 500 g Cu research system. No collector isolation valve, liner, active collector cooling, seal material, or molten-stream trap is documented. |
| **del Rio et al. (2022), university laboratory gas atomizer** — [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1088/1757-899X/1249/1/012034) | A cyclone precedes the bottom powder container; gas vents to atmosphere and large particles enter a water filter. The container is **sealed and handled in a glovebox**. Instrumentation includes pressure transducers, oxygen sensors, gas-flow and nozzle-pressure measurement, thermocouples, and optical pyrometry. (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000013) | Good precedent for sealed handling and comprehensive sensing. The water filter is a separator, not documented collector cooling; container material, seals, isolation valve, and gross-melt protection are unspecified. |
| **Khor (1992), plasma melt and rapid-solidification apparatus** — [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/0924-0136(92)90441-T) | Double-wall stainless chamber with circulating cooling water and a 0–800 °C thermocouple. Water-quenched product passes through a ball valve into filter bags clamped to stainless-steel containers. (pqac-00000014) | Demonstrates water-jacketed stainless construction, temperature measurement, and valved collection, but it is an intentionally **wet quench/filter system**, not a dry inert receiver for partly molten bulk metal. |
| **Tian et al. (2017), Ames calcium centrifugal atomizer** — [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.powtec.2016.12.011) | A rotating bath containing 1,545 cm³ of mechanical-vacuum-pump oil quenched and collected particles; co-rotation reduced impact velocity and distributed heat. During a run, the mild-steel atomization disk failed after about 10 s; atomization continued on its ceramic support. (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000064) | Demonstrates deliberate thermal buffering and a real molten-metal component failure. Oil quenching creates contamination, fire, and compatibility issues and does not establish elastomer or glass receiver performance. |


*Table: Eight documented collection arrangements spanning ultrasonic, gas, plasma, and centrifugal atomizers. The comparison distinguishes demonstrated hardware from a patent proposal and identifies undisclosed seals, ratings, and melt-protection details.*

info.query:
Context. A university lab runs an AMAZEMET rePOWDER ultrasonic atomizer at about 1400 m altitude (room
pressure about 850-865 mbar). A 0.3-1.1 kg charge (aluminium alloys, and copper alloys such as
nickel-aluminium bronze UNS C63000 poured at about 1300 C) is induction-melted in a graphite crucible,
pushed through a 0.5 mm nozzle by argon over-pressure, and falls onto a plate vibrating at 40 kHz that
breaks it into powder (d50 roughly 100 um on good runs). Powder falls through a water-cooled stainless
cone under the chamber into a collection container that hangs from the cone's outlet flange on a
hinged clamp (ISO-KF style with a centring ring and O-ring, or possibly sanitary tri-clamp; size about
DN40-50, being confirmed). The chamber is evacuated to about 10 mbar absolute and backfilled with argon
several times, then runs at about +150 mbar gauge; a mechanical relief valve opens at +0.8 bar.
The stock container, top to bottom: the flange on a short neck, a conical reducer, a valve body with a
lever-operated flap valve whose seat is an EPDM ring, a borosilicate(?) glass tube about 100 mm across
in a perforated steel guard, sealed by elastomer rings in grooves of a top and a bottom stainless plate,
and four tie rods. A curved stainless splash plate sits in the bore at the top. The manufacturer also
supplies protective "shields" that fit in the cone; on the failed run they were not fitted and the
splash plate was in backwards.

The failure (Nov 13 2026): the plate barely atomized, so most of an 816 g C63000 charge left it as 1-3 mm
shot, still partly liquid when it reached the container about 0.4 s later. Bronze piled up at the
container's entrance; the glass glowed orange; the EPDM valve seat burned (white crust, smoke out of
the joint); the seals under the glass were damaged; the glass cracked at its top rim. Good runs never
damaged the container. The manufacturer says a "much simpler metal cup, without the glass" exists
(a stainless tube with a separate sanitary butterfly valve), and that in their own lab they mostly use
"the simple stainless steel" tube because it is easier to make and clean, but its delivery date is
unknown. The lab wants to build its own container within days to a few weeks, glass or metal.

The lab's design so far (to be reviewed, not assumed correct):
A. All-metal, catalogue parts only: a 316L ISO-KF full nipple (bore about 48 mm, 200-250 mm long) hung
   from the cone with the existing clamp; a KF blank flange at the bottom with a stainless centring ring
   and FKM O-ring; a drop-in 304/316 sacrificial liner sleeve in the top bore so that hot metal cannot
   touch the top O-ring; a loose copper or steel "catch puck" at the bottom to soak up heat and keep the
   pile off the bottom joint; Type K thermocouples clamped on the outside at the top flange and near the
   bottom, read by a panel meter with an alarm; no valve (a KF blank and clamp go on the top after
   removal), or a full-port valve whose seats are hidden behind the ball when open.
B. All-metal, turned and TIG-welded: one 316L vessel (KF weld stub, a 63-76 mm tube, a 10 mm welded
   bottom, no bottom seal), with an internal shoulder that locates the sacrificial liner.
C. Glass rebuild: the stock plates, valve and tie rods with a fused-quartz tube in place of the
   borosilicate, FKM or silicone seals, and a stainless liner sleeve that covers the glass rim and the
   top seal.

Find precedents: published designs, manuals, theses, patents or incident reports for powder
collection canisters, cans or cyclones under metal atomizers (gas, ultrasonic, centrifugal, plasma),
especially how they are protected from unatomized molten metal, shot or splats, what materials and
seals they use, whether they have isolation valves, how they are cooled or instrumented, and any
failures where hot metal reached the collection container, melted seals or cracked glass. Include
lab-scale and university-built atomizers. Give citations with DOIs or URLs.
